questions.question: When designing data-intensive applications, which observation explains why applications usually combine several different data systems instead of using one?

options.text: No single tool efficiently serves every way the data is used
Distributed transactions cannot be implemented at all across heterogeneous systems
An append-only log is always cheaper to operate than a database
Batch and stream processing engines have fully converged into one engine

questions.explanation: Every piece of software, even a so-called general-purpose database, is optimized for a particular usage pattern, while a complex application uses the same data in several ways (transactional lookups, keyword search, analytics, caching). So applications compose specialized tools, and the engineering problem becomes data integration: getting data into the right form in all the right places. Distributed transactions across heterogeneous systems do exist (for example XA), but their weaknesses are an argument about how to integrate, not about why integration is needed.

questions.question: Why is a single storage product that tries to support every storage and access approach likely to end up with a poor implementation?

options.text: Making one code path robust and fast is already hard; spreading effort leaves every path weak
A product supporting several approaches cannot be compiled or deployed as one binary
Each storage approach requires the product to be written in a different programming language
Supporting several approaches at once violates the rules of the relational model

questions.explanation: For a problem like storing data and looking it up later there are many valid approaches (log-structured storage, B-trees, column-oriented storage), each appropriate in different circumstances. An implementation typically has to pick one, because getting a single code path robust and performant already takes a great deal of engineering, and the approaches' trade-offs conflict (for example write-optimized versus read-optimized layouts). Trying to do everything in one piece of software almost guarantees a poor implementation, which is why specialized tools are composed instead.

questions.question: Fault-tolerance algorithms, partitioning, and mechanisms for schema evolution and abstraction each serve one of three overarching goals for data-intensive applications. Which three?

options.text: Reliability, scalability, and maintainability
Linearizability, serializability, and durability
Consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Atomicity, isolation, and low latency

questions.explanation: Fault tolerance improves reliability (the system keeps working correctly despite faults), partitioning improves scalability (performance holds as load grows), and evolution and abstraction mechanisms improve maintainability (people can understand and change the system). The distractors are properties of specific mechanisms, such as transaction guarantees or the CAP trade-off, rather than the overall goals those mechanisms serve.

questions.question: Looking beyond reliable, scalable, and maintainable, which set of qualities is proposed as the goal for designing future applications?

options.text: Robust, correct, evolvable, and ultimately beneficial to humanity
Fast, cheap, secure, and as data-driven as possible
Linearizable, serializable, durable, and always available
Robust, correct, highly performant, and as commercially profitable as possible

questions.explanation: The proposed goal is applications that are robust (tolerate faults), correct (well-defined semantics even under faults), evolvable (can change with requirements), and ultimately beneficial to humanity. The last item makes social and ethical impact part of the design goal rather than treating technical or commercial success as sufficient. Linearizable plus always available is not even achievable together under network partitions, and profit is a purpose, not a quality of good design.

questions.question: Across storage engines (log-structured, B-tree, column-oriented) and replication schemes (single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless), what recurring lesson applies?

options.text: Each problem has several solutions with different trade-offs, none best everywhere
One approach eventually dominates every other once workloads are well understood
The newest approach supersedes the older ones for every workload it is applied to
The trade-offs disappear once a system grows to a sufficiently large scale

questions.explanation: For any given problem there are several solutions with different pros, cons, and trade-offs. For example, LSM-trees favour write throughput while B-trees favour predictable reads, and leaderless replication improves availability at the cost of weaker consistency. The right choice depends on circumstances, so the first challenge is mapping software products to the situations they suit; scale tends to sharpen trade-offs rather than remove them.

questions.question: When choosing data systems, what is true even of a so-called general-purpose database?

options.text: It is designed for a particular usage pattern and suits some workloads poorly
It serves every usage pattern about as well as a specialized tool would
It is only a marketing label, with no particular design behind it
It is the correct default for any workload, whatever its access pattern

questions.explanation: Every system is built around assumptions about workload, access patterns, latency, scale, and failure. A general-purpose database covers many common cases, but its design still embodies a particular usage pattern, so some workloads (for example sophisticated full-text search or large analytic scans) fit it poorly. Vendors rarely advertise those poor fits, so engineers must read between the lines using knowledge of the underlying trade-offs.

questions.question: Which pair of systems is commonly integrated so that an application has both a durable system of record and support for queries on arbitrary keywords?

options.text: An OLTP database plus a full-text search index
Two relational databases from different vendors
A cache plus a message broker
A graph database plus a key-value store

questions.explanation: Some databases (such as PostgreSQL) have built-in full-text indexing that suffices for simple applications, but sophisticated search needs specialist information-retrieval tools. Conversely, search indexes are generally not suitable as a durable system of record. So many applications combine an OLTP database (authoritative records and transactions) with a search index (a derived view optimized for keyword queries), which immediately raises the problem of keeping the two in sync.

questions.question: When engineers claim that '99% of people only need X' (or don't need X) about a data-system feature, what does such a claim mostly reveal?

options.text: More about the speaker's own experience than about the feature's usefulness
A statistically robust measurement of needs across many organizations
That most data-system features are genuinely unnecessary
That the need for data integration arises only rarely in practice

questions.explanation: The range of things organizations do with data is extremely wide, so a feature one person considers obscure may be a central requirement for someone else. Such claims generalize from the speaker's own projects. The need for data integration in particular often becomes apparent only when you zoom out and look at dataflows across an entire organization, rather than at a single application.

questions.question: An application writes each change directly to both an OLTP database and a search index (dual writes). What correctness problem can arise?

options.text: Concurrent conflicting writes may be applied in different orders, so the systems diverge
Writes become slower, but the two systems are guaranteed to converge to the same state
The search index rejects each write until the database has confirmed that write first
The database decides the order of both systems' writes, so the index always agrees

questions.explanation: With dual writes, neither system is in charge of the order of writes. If two clients concurrently send conflicting writes, the database may apply them in one order and the search index in the other, and the two can stay permanently inconsistent. The fix is to funnel writes through a single system that decides the order (for example writing to the system of record and deriving the index via change data capture in the same order), so every derived representation processes the writes identically.

questions.question: When a derived data system such as a search index is updated by consuming an event log, which two properties of the updates make recovery from faults easy?

options.text: Determinism and idempotence
Atomicity and durability
Linearizability and serializability
Synchronous acknowledgment and replication

questions.explanation: If the update logic is deterministic, replaying the same events always produces the same derived state; if it is idempotent, applying an event a second time (for example after a crash before the consumer recorded its offset) has no extra effect. Together these let a failed consumer simply restart from an earlier log position and reprocess. Atomicity, durability, linearizability, and serializability are transaction guarantees, which is the different approach that log-based integration is being compared against.

questions.question: Distributed transactions and log-based derived data systems both keep multiple systems consistent. How do their mechanisms for ordering writes and getting exactly-once effects differ?

options.text: Transactions: locks and atomic commit; logs: log order plus deterministic, idempotent retry
Both: locks to decide the order of writes and atomic commit for exactly-once effects
Both: a log to decide the order of writes and idempotent retry for exactly-once effects
Transactions: log order and idempotent retry; logs: locks and atomic commit

questions.explanation: Distributed transactions decide the ordering of writes using locks for mutual exclusion (two-phase locking) and use atomic commit so changes take effect exactly once. Change data capture and event sourcing instead use the position in a log for ordering, and rely on deterministic retry and idempotence for exactly-once effects. The biggest practical difference is timing: transaction systems usually provide linearizability (so you can read your own writes), whereas derived data is usually updated asynchronously and does not offer that by default.

questions.question: What is a balanced assessment of distributed transactions (such as XA) for integrating heterogeneous data systems?

options.text: Useful in limited settings, but XA's fault tolerance and speed are poor
They are the most robust way to integrate any set of heterogeneous systems
They have never worked successfully in any production environment
A better protocol is already widely adopted and integrated with existing tools

questions.explanation: Distributed transactions have been used successfully in limited environments that are willing to pay their cost. But XA has poor fault tolerance and performance, which severely limits its usefulness; a better protocol might be possible, but getting one widely adopted and integrated with existing tools is unlikely to happen soon. Log-based derived data therefore looks most promising, while still recognizing that guarantees like reading your own writes are valuable and should not be dismissed with 'eventual consistency is inevitable'.

questions.question: As systems grow, which situations prevent constructing a single total order of all events? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Partitioning across machines leaves no total order between partitions
Independent datacenter leaders leave cross-datacenter order undefined
Independent microservices have no shared order for their events
Multiple producers destroy ordering even within one log partition

questions.explanation: A totally ordered log usually needs every event to pass through a single leader. That breaks down when throughput forces partitioning (no order between partitions), when each datacenter has its own leader (no order between datacenters), when microservices keep independent durable state (no order between services), and when offline-capable clients update local state (clients and servers see different orders). Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, and most consensus algorithms cannot share the ordering work across nodes.

optionExplanations.a: Each partition can maintain its own ordered log, but events in different partitions have no inherent relative position. A global order would require coordination across all partitions.
optionExplanations.b: Independent leaders in different datacenters serialize local writes separately, so network delay and concurrent acceptance leave cross-datacenter order undefined until reconciliation.
optionExplanations.c: Autonomous services emit events under separate clocks and logs, with no shared sequencer. Causal links must be carried explicitly if consumers need more than local order.
optionExplanations.d: A broker can serialize records from many producers within one partition by assigning offsets at append time. Multiple producers complicate causality but do not inherently destroy partition order.

questions.question: In event-based data integration, when does the lack of a total order of events cause little problem?

options.text: When the events have no causal link, so either order is acceptable
Whenever the events were produced by processes on the same machine
Whenever all of the nodes' clocks are synchronized closely with NTP
Whenever the events concern different objects stored in different places

questions.explanation: Concurrent events with no causal relationship can be ordered either way without changing the outcome. Multiple updates to the same object are also easy: route all updates for an object ID to the same log partition so they are totally ordered. The hard case is a causal dependency between events on different objects or systems, such as an unfriend action followed by a message, which is why 'different objects' is not a safe criterion; clock synchronization cannot reliably recover causal order either.

questions.question: User A removes user B as a friend, then sends a message complaining about B to A's remaining friends. Friendship status and messages are stored in different systems. What can go wrong?

options.text: A notification service may see the message first and still notify B
The message may be lost because both events concern the same pair of users
The unfriend event may be applied twice, deleting A's other friendships
The two systems may deadlock while each waits for the other's event to arrive

questions.explanation: A intends that B not see the message, because it was sent after the friendship was revoked. But if the causal dependency between the unfriend event and the message-send event is not captured, a notification service may see the message first and, still treating B as a friend, notify B. The notification is effectively a join between messages and the friend list, so it suffers from the time-dependence of joins; there is no simple general answer.

questions.question: Which approaches are suggested as partial remedies for capturing causal dependencies between events when total order broadcast is not feasible? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Logical timestamps, which order events without coordination but need recipients to handle out-of-order delivery
Logging the state a user saw as an event with a unique ID, which later events reference
Conflict resolution algorithms, which help maintain state but not with external side effects
Synchronized physical clocks, from whose timestamps causal order can be read directly

questions.explanation: There does not seem to be a simple answer to capturing causality across systems, but there are starting points. Logical timestamps give a total order without coordination, at the cost of extra metadata and handling out-of-order arrival. Recording what the user saw as an identified event lets later events cite it explicitly. Conflict resolution handles events arriving in an unexpected order for stored state, though not for side effects such as notifications. Physical clocks cannot reliably capture causality.

optionExplanations.a: Logical timestamps such as sequence numbers provide a total ordering without coordination, so they help where total order broadcast is infeasible. Recipients must still cope with events arriving out of order, and extra metadata must travel with each event.
optionExplanations.b: If the event recording what the user saw before deciding has a unique identifier, any later event can reference it, making the causal dependency explicit instead of inferring it from timing.
optionExplanations.c: Conflict resolution algorithms make state converge even when events arrive in an unexpected order. They do not help once an action has external side effects, such as a notification already sent to a user.
optionExplanations.d: Clock synchronization via NTP has errors that grow during pauses, faults, and network delay, so physical timestamp order cannot reliably reconstruct which event caused which.

questions.question: When applications combine multiple specialized data systems, what is the goal of data integration?

options.text: Making sure data ends up in the right form in all the right places
Storing all of an organization's data in one single database
Eliminating derived data in favour of one canonical copy
Making every system in the organization linearizable

questions.explanation: Data integration means getting each piece of data into every system that needs it, in the representation that system needs. That requires consuming inputs, transforming, joining, filtering, aggregating, training models, evaluating, and writing to the appropriate outputs, and batch and stream processors are the tools for this. Their outputs are derived datasets such as search indexes, materialized views, recommendations, and aggregate metrics, so derived data is embraced rather than eliminated.

questions.question: What is the main fundamental difference between batch processing and stream processing?

options.text: Stream input is unbounded; batch input is finite and known in size
Batch jobs are deterministic, while stream jobs cannot be deterministic
Batch jobs read from HDFS, while stream jobs can read only from Kafka
Stream jobs have lower latency, and latency alone defines the two categories

questions.explanation: Batch and stream processing share many principles; the fundamental difference is that a batch job's input is finite and known, while a stream processor's input never ends. Implementation differences are blurring: Spark performs stream processing by breaking a stream into microbatches, and Apache Flink performs batch processing on a stream engine, though performance differs (for example microbatching can do poorly with hopping or sliding windows). Stream processors can be deterministic too, and both kinds can read from various sources.

questions.question: Which description best captures the 'functional flavour' of batch processing?

options.text: Deterministic, side-effect-free functions over immutable inputs, with append-only outputs
Long-running stateful jobs that update shared records in place as they process input
Jobs that only qualify if they are written in a functional programming language
Procedures whose output depends on the wall-clock time at which each one happens to run

questions.explanation: Batch processing encourages pure, deterministic functions whose output depends only on their input, with no side effects other than explicit outputs, treating inputs as immutable and outputs as append-only, whatever language the code is written in. Stream processing is similar but adds managed, fault-tolerant state. Deterministic functions with well-defined inputs and outputs help fault tolerance (rerun on failure) and make dataflows across an organization easier to reason about.

questions.question: Derived data could be maintained synchronously, as a relational database updates a secondary index within the same transaction. Why do event-log-based systems prefer asynchronous maintenance?

options.text: A fault stays local, whereas a distributed transaction aborts if any node fails
Synchronous maintenance of derived data across several systems cannot be implemented
Asynchrony gives every reader of the derived data lower latency and fresher results
Asynchronous maintenance guarantees that every user can read their own writes immediately

questions.explanation: Asynchrony is what makes event-log-based systems robust: if one consumer fails, the log buffers events and the rest of the system keeps running, so the fault stays local. Distributed transactions abort if any participant fails, so they amplify failures. The same applies to secondary indexes in a partitioned system, which need cross-partition writes (term-partitioned) or reads (document-partitioned); that communication is most reliable and scalable when the index is maintained asynchronously. The cost is weaker timing guarantees, not stronger ones.

questions.question: When maintaining derived data, what does each of stream processing and batch processing contribute?

options.text: Streaming reflects input changes with low delay; batch reprocesses accumulated history
Batch reflects input changes with low delay; streaming reprocesses accumulated history
Both reflect new input with low delay; neither can reprocess accumulated history
Both reprocess accumulated history; neither can reflect new input with low delay

questions.explanation: Stream processing propagates changes into derived views quickly, while batch processing can reprocess large amounts of historical data to derive entirely new views of an existing dataset. Reprocessing matters for evolution: without it, schema changes are limited to simple additions such as a new optional field or record type (in both schema-on-write and schema-on-read systems); with it, a dataset can be restructured into a completely different model to serve new requirements.

questions.question: After England standardized railway gauge in 1846, lines were converted gradually by adding a third rail so trains of both gauges could run. Why do nonstandard gauges, such as on San Francisco's BART system, still exist?

options.text: Conversion is possible but expensive, so some lines were never converted
Converting a line's gauge proved to be technically impossible
Dual-gauge track prevents trains of either gauge from running safely
The standard gauge was later abandoned in favour of wider gauges

questions.explanation: Dual or mixed gauge lets old and new trains share a line during a gradual migration, after which the extra rail can be removed. This is a physical analogy for schema migration: keep old and new versions side by side and shift traffic over time. The approach works but is an expensive undertaking, so some nonstandard gauges persist, just as some data migrations are never completed because their cost outweighs their benefit.

questions.question: How do derived views allow a dataset to be restructured gradually instead of through a sudden switch?

options.text: Keep old and new schemas as two views of the same data, moving users over gradually
Rewrite all of the data in place in one migration, then switch every user at once
Take the system offline until the new schema has been fully backfilled from the old one
Convert the underlying event log destructively to the new format before anything else

questions.explanation: Because both schemas are derived from the same underlying data, they can be maintained side by side. A small fraction of users can be routed to the new view to test its performance and find bugs, then the fraction increased until the old view can be dropped. Every stage is easily reversible because a working system remains available, which reduces the risk of irreversible damage and lets teams move faster.

questions.question: In the lambda architecture, how is incoming data recorded and how are views produced from it?

options.text: Immutable events are appended; batch and stream systems each derive views from them
Writes update a database in place, and a stream processor maintains a cache alongside it
Two identical stream processors consume the input in parallel, one as a hot standby
One unified engine runs the same code for both historical and live data

questions.explanation: The lambda architecture records input by appending immutable events, similar to event sourcing, and derives read-optimized views from them using two systems in parallel: a stream processor (such as Storm) quickly produces approximate updates, and a batch processor (such as Hadoop MapReduce) later reprocesses the same events to produce a corrected view. The rationale was that batch processing is simpler and less bug-prone and can use exact algorithms. A single engine for both is the later 'unified' approach, not lambda.

questions.question: Despite its practical problems, what lasting contribution did the lambda architecture make to data system design?

options.text: It popularized deriving views from immutable events and reprocessing them as needed
It proved that stream processors are inherently more reliable than batch processors
It removed the need for batch processing in data pipelines altogether
It showed that one codebase can automatically run unchanged in both batch and streaming

questions.explanation: The lambda architecture shaped data systems for the better by popularizing two principles: record input as immutable events and derive read-optimized views from them, and reprocess the events when the derived views need correcting or changing. Its problems lie in running two systems, the batch layer and the speed layer, rather than in those principles; libraries such as Summingbird abstract the shared logic, but the operational burden of two systems remains.

questions.question: Which practical problems does the lambda architecture, which runs a batch layer and a stream layer side by side, have? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Batch and streaming paths duplicate implementation and operations
Their separate outputs are difficult to merge for complex views
Frequent reprocessing is expensive, so incremental batches add complexity
The architecture cannot express joins or sessionization

questions.explanation: Maintaining the same logic in both a batch and a streaming framework is significant extra effort, and the operational complexity of two systems remains even with shared abstractions. The two layers produce separate outputs that must be merged, which is easy for simple tumbling-window aggregations but hard for joins, sessionization, or non-time-series outputs. And reprocessing all history frequently is expensive, so batch jobs become incremental, which reintroduces stragglers and window-boundary problems and makes the batch layer as complex as the streaming one.

optionExplanations.a: Maintaining separate batch and speed implementations duplicates business logic, deployment, and operations. The two paths can evolve differently and produce inconsistent interpretations.
optionExplanations.b: Simple counters may merge, but complex joins or models from two engines can be hard to reconcile into one authoritative view. Users may observe disagreement between paths.
optionExplanations.c: Repeated full-history batch runs become expensive as history grows; making them incremental introduces state, windows, and recovery concerns similar to stream processing.
optionExplanations.d: Both batch and stream engines can express joins and session windows. Lambda's drawback is duplicated paths and reconciliation, not an inability to represent those operations.

questions.question: Which features let a single system handle both reprocessing of history and live stream processing, providing lambda's benefits without its two code paths? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Replay historical events through the same engine used for live events
Use exactly-once effects so retries do not change results
Window by event time so historical replay remains meaningful
Add a second batch layer solely to correct the first batch layer

questions.explanation: Unifying batch and stream processing in one system needs three features: the ability to replay historical events through the same engine that handles recent events (for example from a log-based broker, or from HDFS); exactly-once semantics, so the output is the same as if no faults had occurred, which requires discarding partial output of failed tasks; and windowing by event time rather than processing time, since processing time is meaningless when reprocessing history (Apache Beam expresses this, run on Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow). Adding more batch layers would only multiply lambda's duplication.

optionExplanations.a: A replayable log lets one implementation process both retained history and new events. Corrections can rebuild state without maintaining a separate batch codebase.
optionExplanations.b: Exactly-once effects or equivalent idempotence make retries and historical replay converge on the same result. Without duplicate control, rebuilding could apply events twice.
optionExplanations.c: Event-time windows use timestamps from the events, so replaying old data reproduces the original grouping instead of assigning everything to the current processing time.
optionExplanations.d: A second batch layer recreates the duplicate implementations and merge problem lambda already has. The goal is one replay-capable engine, not another correction path.

questions.question: At the most abstract level, what functions do databases, Hadoop, and operating systems with their filesystems have in common?

options.text: They store data and allow you to process and query it
They provide multi-object transactions and a query optimizer
They expose all stored data through a SQL query interface
They store all data only as untyped sequences of bytes

questions.explanation: Databases, Hadoop, and operating systems are all information-management systems: they store data and let you process and query it. A database stores records in a data model (rows, documents, graph vertices), while a filesystem stores files; Hadoop is somewhat like a distributed Unix. Practical differences remain, such as filesystems coping poorly with 10 million small files in a directory while a database with 10 million small records is unremarkable.

questions.question: How did Unix and relational databases differ in the level of abstraction they offered programmers?

options.text: Unix: a fairly low-level hardware abstraction; databases: a high-level one hiding storage
Unix: a high-level abstraction hiding storage; databases: a fairly low-level hardware one
Both offered the same low-level abstraction of files and of pipes carrying raw bytes
Both hid concurrency control and crash recovery behind a high-level declarative query language

questions.explanation: Unix presented programmers with a logical but fairly low-level abstraction of the hardware: files and pipes that are just sequences of bytes. Relational databases gave application programmers a high-level abstraction (SQL and transactions) that hides on-disk data structures, concurrency, and crash recovery. Each is 'simpler' in a different sense: Unix as a thin wrapper around hardware resources, relational databases because a short declarative query draws on powerful infrastructure (query optimization, indexes, join methods, concurrency control, replication) without whoever writes the query needing to understand its implementation.

questions.question: How can the NoSQL movement be interpreted in terms of the long-running tension between the Unix and relational database philosophies?

options.text: As applying a Unix-like approach of low-level abstractions to distributed OLTP storage
As applying the relational approach of high-level declarative queries to new data models
As finally resolving the tension in favour of the relational philosophy
As abandoning both philosophies in favour of an unrelated third approach

questions.explanation: Both Unix and the relational model emerged in the early 1970s, and the tension between their philosophies has lasted for decades without resolution. NoSQL stores typically expose simpler, lower-level primitives (such as key-value access) and leave more to the application, which mirrors the Unix preference for low-level building blocks, applied to distributed OLTP data storage. Unbundled databases attempt to reconcile the two philosophies.

questions.question: When a relational database runs CREATE INDEX on a table without locking it against writes, what does it do?

options.text: Index a consistent snapshot, apply writes made since, then keep the index up to date
Lock the table, build the index in a single pass, and rebuild it from scratch every night
Build nothing up front, computing index entries lazily as each query arrives
Index only rows written after the command, leaving existing rows unindexed

questions.explanation: The database scans a consistent snapshot of the table, picks out and sorts the indexed field values, and writes the index; it then processes the backlog of writes made since the snapshot, and from then on updates the index whenever a transaction writes to the table. This is remarkably similar to setting up a new follower replica, and to bootstrapping change data capture with an initial snapshot. In effect CREATE INDEX reprocesses the existing dataset to derive a new view of it.

questions.question: What is meant by viewing an organization's dataflows as a 'meta-database of everything'?

options.text: Data-moving batch, stream, and ETL jobs act like one database maintaining indexes and views
Every organization should consolidate all of its data onto one physical database
Databases should be replaced throughout the organization by one shared distributed filesystem
ETL processes become unnecessary once an organization reaches sufficient scale

questions.explanation: Whenever a batch, stream, or ETL process moves data from one place and form to another, it behaves like the database subsystem that keeps indexes or materialized views up to date. Batch and stream processors resemble elaborate triggers, stored procedures, and view-maintenance routines, and the derived systems they maintain resemble different index types. The difference is that these facilities are provided by separate software, on different machines, run by different teams, rather than by one integrated product.

questions.question: Federated databases and unbundled databases are two ways to compose diverse storage systems into a cohesive whole. What does each unify?

options.text: Federation unifies reads; unbundling unifies writes
Federation unifies the writes and unbundling unifies the reads
Each of the two addresses only the reading of data
Each of the two addresses only the writing of data

questions.explanation: A federated database (polystore), such as PostgreSQL with foreign data wrappers, offers one query interface over many storage engines, following the relational tradition of a single high-level language. Unbundling uses change data capture and event logs to make every data change reach all the right systems, following the Unix tradition of small tools composed through a uniform low-level interface. Federated read-only querying is mainly a data-model mapping problem; keeping writes in sync is the harder engineering problem.

questions.question: What is the traditional approach to keeping writes synchronized across heterogeneous storage systems?

options.text: Distributed transactions, such as XA two-phase commit, spanning the systems
An asynchronous event log consumed by idempotent writers in each system
A federated query layer that unifies reads across the systems
Leaderless quorum replication between the different storage products

questions.explanation: The traditional approach uses distributed transactions across the heterogeneous systems. That is considered the wrong solution there: transactions within one storage or stream-processing system work, but across technologies built by different groups there is no widely adopted transaction protocol, and XA has poor fault tolerance and performance. The proposed alternative is an ordered event log with idempotent consumers, a simpler abstraction that is more feasible to implement across heterogeneous systems. Federation unifies reads, not writes.

questions.question: Log-based integration of data systems gives loose coupling between components. At which levels does that loose coupling show up? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: System-level buffering isolates producers and healthy consumers from failures
Team-level boundaries let components evolve through durable event interfaces
Hardware-level coupling disappears because no network is required
Legal liability moves away from the operator of the composed system

questions.explanation: At the system level, asynchronous event streams make the whole more robust: if a consumer is slow or fails, the log buffers messages so producers and other consumers continue, and the faulty consumer catches up later without missing data. At the human level, unbundling lets different teams develop, improve, and maintain components independently, with the event log as a well-defined interface that is general yet preserves ordering and durability. Synchronous distributed transactions instead escalate local faults into large-scale failures.

optionExplanations.a: A durable log absorbs a consumer outage while producers and unrelated consumers continue. The failed consumer later resumes from its offset instead of coupling everyone to its availability.
optionExplanations.b: Stable event contracts let producer and consumer teams deploy on different schedules and add new derived views independently. The log becomes an organizational boundary as well as a buffer.
optionExplanations.c: Log-based integration still relies on networks and storage hardware; it manages failure coupling rather than making physical dependencies disappear. No-network operation is not the claimed benefit.
optionExplanations.d: Technical decoupling does not automatically transfer legal or ethical responsibility away from the system operator. Liability depends on governance and law, not message topology.

questions.question: What is the goal of unbundling databases, that is, composing specialized storage and processing tools?

options.text: Good performance across many more workloads than any single product handles
Beating each specialized database on its own benchmark workload, one product at a time
Replacing databases entirely with event logs and stream processors throughout the system
Reaching the maximum possible optimization depth for one particular kind of workload

questions.explanation: Unbundling is about breadth, not depth: combining several databases to perform well across many workloads, not outperforming any one database on the workload it was designed for. Databases are still needed for stream-processor state and for serving outputs. Each extra component adds learning curve, configuration, and operational quirks, and an integrated product can be faster and more predictable for its target workload, so if one product does everything you need, use it; compose only when no single product suffices.

questions.question: For unbundled databases composed from storage and processing systems, what major piece is considered still missing?

options.text: A high-level declarative language for composing them, like a Unix shell
A log-based message broker that can durably retain old messages and replay them on demand
A mechanism to capture every change made to a database as a stream of change events
A secondary-index data structure that can be updated incrementally as new writes arrive

questions.explanation: The tools exist (replayable log brokers, change data capture, incremental indexes), but there is no unbundled equivalent of the Unix shell for declaring how they compose. The aspiration is something like 'mysql | elasticsearch': an unbundled CREATE INDEX that indexes all existing MySQL documents in Elasticsearch and then continually applies every change without custom code. Similarly, caches could be declared as materialized views; research such as differential dataflow explores this.

questions.question: What name has become attached to the approach of unbundling databases by composing specialized storage and processing systems with application code?

options.text: The 'database inside-out' approach
The lambda architecture
The federated database, or polystore, approach
The shared-nothing architecture

questions.explanation: The name comes from a 2014 conference talk titled 'Turning the Database Inside-out'. It is better seen as a design pattern than a new architecture, and it amalgamates earlier ideas from dataflow languages (Oz, Juttle), functional reactive programming (Elm), and logic programming (Bloom); the term 'unbundling' was proposed by Jay Kreps. The lambda architecture is a specific batch-plus-stream design, and federation unifies reads rather than turning a database's internals into composable dataflow.

questions.question: Which spreadsheet capability is exactly what derived-data systems want at the level of a whole data system?

options.text: Automatic recalculation whenever any input to a formula changes
Static type checking of the values flowing between cells
Transactional isolation between concurrent cell updates
Distributed execution of a formula across many machines

questions.explanation: In a spreadsheet, a formula in one cell is automatically recalculated whenever any of its inputs change. At the data-system level, the equivalent is that when a record changes, every index, cached view, and aggregation depending on it is automatically refreshed, without the developer worrying about how. Unlike spreadsheets, data systems must also be fault-tolerant, scalable, and durable, and must integrate technologies written by different people over time.

questions.question: How do the derivation functions for a secondary index and a full-text search index differ?

options.text: Secondary: sort the indexed field values; full-text: linguistic processing into an inverted index
Both apply linguistic processing such as stemming and synonym detection to their input
Both simply pick out and sort the values of the indexed field, with nothing else
Secondary: stemming and synonym detection; full-text: a plain sort of each document's text field

questions.explanation: A secondary index has a straightforward transformation: for each row or document, pick out the values of the indexed columns and sort by them (for a B-tree or SSTable index). A full-text index applies natural-language processing such as language detection, word segmentation, stemming or lemmatization, spelling correction, and synonym identification, then builds a lookup structure such as an inverted index. Both are derivation functions; they differ in how standard and how application-specific they are.

questions.question: Which derivation functions do databases typically build in, and which usually require custom application code?

options.text: Secondary indexing is built in; ML feature engineering needs custom code
Every derivation, including machine-learning feature engineering, is built into databases
None is built in; even secondary indexes require custom application code to maintain
ML feature engineering is built in; secondary indexes require custom application code

questions.explanation: Secondary indexing is needed so commonly that databases provide it as a core feature invoked with CREATE INDEX. Full-text indexing is partly built in for common languages but sophisticated features need domain-specific tuning. Machine-learning feature engineering is notoriously application-specific. When a derivation is not cookie-cutter, custom code is required, and that is where databases struggle: triggers, stored procedures, and user-defined functions have been somewhat of an afterthought in database design.

questions.question: Databases could in theory host arbitrary application code through stored procedures. Which kind of tool is better suited to running application code?

options.text: Cluster managers and containers such as Mesos, YARN, Docker, and Kubernetes
Stored procedures, which give the best versioning and dependency management
Database triggers, which integrate most easily with external network services
User-defined functions, which make rolling upgrades and monitoring simplest

questions.explanation: In practice databases are poorly suited as deployment environments: they fit badly with dependency and package management, version control, rolling upgrades, evolvability, monitoring, metrics, calls to network services, and integration with external systems. Deployment and cluster-management tools are designed specifically for running code and, by doing one thing well, do it much better. So some parts of a system should specialize in durable data storage and others in running application code, interacting while remaining independent.

questions.question: Functional programmers joke about 'the separation of Church and state'. Which deployment pattern does this describe, and where is the pun?

options.text: Stateless app logic kept apart from a stateful database; Church is Alonzo Church
Stateful applications paired with stateless databases; Church refers to Edgar Codd
All state kept inside the application process; Church refers to Alan Turing
Application logic placed in the database as stored procedures; Church is Alonzo Church

questions.explanation: Most web applications run as stateless services (any request can go to any server, which forgets it afterwards) with persistent state kept in a database: no application logic in the database and no persistent state in the application. Alonzo Church created the lambda calculus, the basis of functional programming, which has no mutable state, hence the pun on separation of church and state. In this model the database acts like a mutable shared variable accessed synchronously over the network.

questions.question: In the typical web-application model the database acts like a mutable shared variable. What limitation of mutable variables have databases inherited?

options.text: Readers cannot subscribe to changes, so they must poll to detect them
Readers cannot read the value while a writer is updating it
Every change automatically notifies all readers, flooding them with updates
Values cannot be made durable, so they are lost when a process crashes

questions.explanation: In most programming languages you cannot subscribe to changes in a mutable variable, only read it periodically; notifications require implementing the observer pattern yourself. Databases inherited this passive model: to find out whether content has changed, the usual option is to repeat the query (poll). Subscribing to changes, such as change streams, is only beginning to emerge as a database feature, and it is what dataflow-oriented applications need.

questions.question: What relationship does designing applications around dataflow renegotiate?

options.text: The relationship between application code and state management
The relationship between clients and servers over the network
The division between data stored on disk and data held in memory
The choice between relational and document data models

questions.explanation: Instead of treating the database as a passive variable manipulated by the application, dataflow thinking focuses on the interplay between state, state changes, and the code that processes them: application code responds to state changes in one place by triggering state changes in another. Precedents include subscribing to a database's change log as a stream, actor-based message passing, tuple spaces, database triggers, and secondary-index maintenance; unbundling applies this to derived datasets outside the primary database.

questions.question: Why is maintaining derived data via messaging not the same as the asynchronous job execution that message brokers were traditionally designed for? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The order of state changes matters, so views derived from a log must process events in the same order
Losing a single message leaves the derived dataset permanently out of sync with its source
Derived data must be updated synchronously inside the source system's transaction
Derived-data maintenance and job queues have identical ordering and reliability needs

questions.explanation: Two requirements set derived-data maintenance apart. Ordering: several views derived from one log must process events in the same order to stay consistent with each other, which many brokers violate when redelivering unacknowledged messages, and dual writes are ruled out. Fault tolerance: a single lost message permanently corrupts the derived dataset, so delivery and state updates must both be reliable (unlike actor systems that keep state in memory). These demands are stringent but much cheaper and more robust than distributed transactions, and modern stream processors meet them at scale.

optionExplanations.a: If two views apply the same events in different orders, concurrent updates can leave them permanently inconsistent with each other. Many traditional brokers reorder messages when redelivering unacknowledged ones, which is acceptable for independent jobs but not for derived state.
optionExplanations.b: A lost derivation event is not merely late: the target view stays wrong forever after the source moves on. Reliable delivery plus reliable state updates are therefore integrity requirements, not just conveniences.
optionExplanations.c: The point of log-based derivation is that updates happen asynchronously, outside the source transaction, which contains faults locally. Requiring synchronous in-transaction updates would bring back distributed transactions.
optionExplanations.d: Traditional job queues tolerate reordering on redelivery and often keep state in memory, because individual jobs are independent. Derived views need stable ordering and no loss, so the requirements genuinely differ.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of a service-oriented (microservices) architecture over a single monolithic application?

options.text: Organizational scalability: loosely coupled teams deploy independently
Lower request latency, because each request is handled by a smaller, faster process
Lower hardware cost, because many small services can be packed more densely onto machines
Stronger consistency guarantees between the data held by the different services

questions.explanation: Breaking functionality into services that communicate via synchronous requests such as REST mainly buys organizational scalability through loose coupling: different teams work on different services with less coordination, as long as services can be deployed and updated independently. Composing stream operators into dataflow systems shares much of this, but its communication is one-directional asynchronous message streams rather than synchronous request/response, which also improves fault tolerance and performance.

questions.question: A purchase is priced in one currency but paid in another, so the current exchange rate is needed. How does a dataflow design obtain the rate, compared with a microservices design?

options.text: It subscribes to rate updates in advance and queries a local copy instead of a rate service
It queries the exchange-rate service synchronously over the network for each purchase
It sends the purchase to the exchange-rate service, which converts the price and forwards it
It requires the client to supply the current exchange rate along with the purchase

questions.explanation: In the microservices approach, the purchase-processing code queries an exchange-rate service or database for each purchase. In the dataflow approach, it subscribes to a stream of rate updates, records the current rate in a local database whenever it changes, and queries only that local store when processing a purchase. Replacing a synchronous network request with a local query is faster and more robust to the rate service failing; it amounts to a stream-table join between purchase events and rate-update events. A locally cached rate in the microservice would itself need polling or a change subscription to stay fresh.

questions.question: A stream of purchase events is joined with a stream of exchange-rate updates to convert prices. Why is this join time-dependent?

options.text: Reprocessing later needs the rate at purchase time, not today's rate
Rate updates arrive faster than purchases, so the join must drop some events
Only the dataflow design is affected; querying a rate service avoids the issue
The join must wait for the next rate update before it can emit any output

questions.explanation: If purchase events are reprocessed later, the exchange rate will have changed since the original purchase, so joining against the current rate gives a different answer. Reconstructing the original output requires the historical rate valid at the purchase time. This time dependence must be handled whether the rate comes from querying a service or from subscribing to an update stream; it is one of the open questions around time-dependent joins.

questions.question: In a system that maintains derived datasets such as search indexes, what are the write path and the read path?

options.text: Write path: eager work as data arrives; read path: work done only on request
Write path: the network hop to the server; read path: the disk seek on the server
Write path: always synchronous by definition; read path: always asynchronous by definition
The same sequence of processing steps, traversed in opposite directions

questions.explanation: The write path covers everything done when data is written, possibly through several stages of batch and stream processing, until every derived dataset incorporates it, whether or not anyone has asked for it. The read path is the work done when serving a request: reading from the derived dataset, perhaps processing further, and building the response. The write path resembles eager evaluation and the read path lazy evaluation, and the derived dataset is where the two meet, representing a trade-off between work at write time and at read time.

questions.question: With a full-text search index, what work do the write path and the read path each do?

options.text: Writes update each term's index entries; reads look up terms and apply Boolean logic
Writes precompute results for every possible query; reads only fetch the stored answer
Writes store raw documents unindexed; reads scan every document as grep would
Writes sort documents by timestamp; reads binary-search the documents by date

questions.explanation: Both paths do work. Each document write must update the index entries for all terms it contains; each query must look up every query word and combine results with Boolean logic (AND for all words, OR for synonyms). With no index, writes are cheap but every query scans all documents; precomputing results for every possible query would make reads trivial but is infeasible because the set of possible queries is unbounded. The index sits between these extremes.

questions.question: Between scanning all documents for each search and precomputing results for every possible query, what intermediate design is practical besides a plain index?

options.text: Precompute results for the most common queries only, serving the rest from the index
Precompute results for every possible query and store them as a materialized view
Precompute nothing and scan every document for each query, as grep does
Precompute only the most recent minute's queries and discard the index

questions.explanation: Precomputing every possible query is infeasible, but the most common queries can be precomputed so they are served without touching the index, while uncommon queries still use the index. This is usually called a cache of common queries, but it could also be called a materialized view, since it must be updated when new documents match those queries. Caches, indexes, and materialized views all shift the boundary between the write path and the read path.

questions.question: Which well-known design shifts work from the read path to the write path by precomputing each user's results ahead of time?

options.text: Fanning out each new tweet into followers' cached home timelines
Scanning web server logs with a MapReduce job to count page views
Merging conflicting shopping-cart versions when the cart is read
Checking for write skew when on-call doctors request to go off call

questions.explanation: Twitter's home timelines can be computed at read time by merging recent tweets from everyone a user follows, or at write time by inserting each new tweet into every follower's timeline cache. The fan-out design does more work per write so that reading a timeline is cheap, and the boundary can be drawn differently for celebrities with huge follower counts than for ordinary users. Merging carts on read and log scans put work on the read or batch side instead.

questions.question: Traditionally, what was about the only useful thing a web browser could do without an internet connection?

options.text: Scroll through a page that had already been loaded while online
Submit forms, which the browser queued and sent once back online
Run queries against a local copy of the website's database
Receive server updates that the operating system had cached

questions.explanation: Browsers were stateless clients that could do little offline. Single-page JavaScript apps changed that with client-side interaction and persistent local storage, and mobile apps similarly store much state on the device. This enables offline-first applications that use a local database, work without a connection, and sync with servers in the background, a big advantage on slow or unreliable mobile networks.

questions.question: For a client app that keeps state on the user's device, how can the layers of state be described in derived-data terms?

options.text: Pixels are a materialized view of client objects, which are a replica of server state
The screen is the system of record, and the datacenter keeps a cache of it
The client's model objects are the only authoritative copy of the data
Pixels, client model, and server state are independent copies, none derived from another

questions.explanation: Once state lives on end-user devices, on-device state can be seen as a cache of state on the server: the pixels on the screen are a materialized view of model objects in the client app, and those model objects are a local replica of state in a remote datacenter. Seeing the layers as derived views suggests propagating changes through them like any other dataflow, instead of treating the client as a stateless renderer.

questions.question: In a typical web page, why doesn't the browser learn about data that changes on the server after the page has loaded?

options.text: It reads the data once without subscribing to updates, so its copy goes stale
Browsers cannot keep a TCP connection open to a server after loading a page
HTTP caching rules forbid the browser from re-requesting data it has already cached
The server has no way to know which data the page displayed

questions.explanation: The browser reads data at one point in time and assumes it is static; it does not subscribe to updates, so it finds out about changes only when the page is reloaded or the client polls. Feed protocols like RSS are just a basic form of polling. Server-sent events (the EventSource API) and WebSockets let a browser keep an open TCP connection over which the server pushes messages, reducing the staleness of client-side state.

questions.question: In write-path/read-path terms, what does actively pushing state changes from the server to client devices amount to?

options.text: Extending the write path all the way to the end user's device
Extending the read path all the way back into the server
Moving all precomputation out of the write path into client reads
Replacing the write path with periodic polling by each client

questions.explanation: When the server pushes every state change to devices, the eager, precomputing write path continues past the datacenter right up to the user's screen. A client still uses a read path to fetch its initial state, but afterwards relies on a stream of changes. Devices are offline at times, but the technique of consumer offsets in log-based brokers handles this: each device is a small subscriber that resumes from its last position after reconnecting, without missing messages.

questions.question: Which client-side tools already manage UI state by subscribing to a stream of events (user input and server responses), structured like event sourcing?

options.text: The Elm language, and Facebook's React with Flux and Redux
jQuery, which updates the page directly in each request/response handler
RSS readers, which poll each subscribed feed at fixed intervals
Server-rendered pages that are reloaded on every user interaction

questions.explanation: Elm and the React/Flux/Redux toolchain derive client-side state by processing a stream of events, much as event sourcing derives database state from a log. Extending this model so that servers push state-change events into the same client pipeline would create an end-to-end write path: from an interaction on one device, through event logs and derived systems, to another person's screen, with delays of perhaps under a second. Polling and full reloads are request/response patterns instead.

questions.question: A stream processor writes derived data into a store (database, cache, or index) that serves user queries. What does the store provide that the event log alone does not?

options.text: Random-access lookups that would otherwise mean scanning the whole log
A total order of events, which the log itself cannot provide
Durability of events, which the log itself cannot provide
Replay of historical events, which a log discards once consumers have read them

questions.explanation: The store is the boundary between the write path and the read path: it lets queries look up specific data directly instead of scanning the entire event log. Ordering, durability, and replay are properties the log already provides. Stream processors also keep state for aggregations and joins, and some frameworks let outside clients query that state, turning the stream processor into a simple database.

questions.question: Writes to a store typically go through an event log while reads are transient requests sent directly to storage nodes. What alternative treatment of reads is proposed?

options.text: Represent reads as events too, routed with writes through a stream processor that replies
Serve every read by scanning the event log directly, so that no separate store is needed
Collect the reads into batches and serve all of them in a nightly batch processing job
Forbid one-off reads entirely, so that clients can only hold long-lived subscriptions

questions.explanation: Read requests can be represented as a stream of events and routed, together with write events, to the same stream operator, which responds by emitting the read result to an output stream. This is in effect a stream-table join between the stream of queries and the database, so each read event must be routed to the partition holding the relevant data, just as joins copartition inputs by key. One-off reads and subscriptions both fit this model.

questions.question: When read requests are treated as events joined against a database, how does a one-off read differ from a subscription?

options.text: A one-off read forgets the request; a subscription is a persistent join
Each of the two is a persistent join against future events
Each of the two is a transient join that is then forgotten
A subscription is implemented as repeated point reads, so the server retains no join state

questions.explanation: Serving requests corresponds closely to performing joins. A one-off read passes through the join operator once, produces its result, and is forgotten. A subscription is a persistent join: it stays in place, matching both past state and future changes on the other side of the join, so each later change relevant to the subscriber produces new output pushed to the client.

questions.question: What does recording a durable log of read events provide, and at what cost?

options.text: Better causality and provenance tracking, at extra storage and I/O cost
Smaller event-log storage, at the cost of slower reads for common queries
Faster reads for common queries, at the cost of weaker write consistency
Stronger durability for writes, at the cost of higher write latency

questions.explanation: Logging reads lets you reconstruct what a user saw before making a decision. For example, in an online shop the predicted shipping date and stock status shown to a customer may affect whether they buy, and analyzing that requires recording the result of their query. This improves causality and provenance tracking but adds storage and I/O overhead; reducing it is an open research problem. If read requests are already logged for operational reasons, making that log the source of the requests is a small change.

questions.question: When is routing queries through a stream processor (treating reads as events) probably overkill, and when does it pay off?

options.text: Overkill for single-partition queries; useful for queries combining many partitions
Overkill for queries combining many partitions; useful for single-partition lookups
Always overkill, since a conventional database handles every query better
Never overkill, since it is cheaper than a direct query even for one partition

questions.explanation: For a query touching one partition, sending it through a stream and collecting a response stream adds needless machinery. For complex queries combining data from several partitions, the stream processor's existing infrastructure for routing, partitioning, and joining can be used. Storm's distributed RPC was used to compute how many people saw a URL on Twitter (the union of follower sets of everyone who tweeted it). For such multi-partition joins a database that provides the feature is usually simpler, but queries-as-streams help applications that exceed off-the-shelf solutions.

questions.question: To assess fraud risk for a purchase, a system needs reputation scores for the buyer's IP address, email, billing and shipping addresses, each stored in a differently partitioned database. How can a stream processor gather them?

options.text: As a sequence of joins, routing the event to each dataset's partition
As one join against a single partition that holds all of the reputation data together
As a distributed transaction that locks every partition of every reputation database at once
By copying all of the reputation databases into each incoming purchase event beforehand

questions.explanation: Each reputation database is partitioned by a different key (IP address, email, address), so collecting all scores requires a sequence of joins with differently partitioned datasets: the purchase event is routed to the right partition of the first dataset, then on to the next. Stream processors already provide this routing and joining infrastructure. MPP databases' internal query execution graphs look similar, and if a database offers such multi-partition joins it is usually simpler to use it.

questions.question: Why do stateful systems such as databases need more careful thought about correctness than stateless services that only read data?

options.text: They remember data indefinitely, so a bug's effects can persist instead of vanishing on restart
They are measurably slower to operate, so any performance bug becomes far more costly to users
They cannot be upgraded with rolling deployments, so every fix takes much longer to ship
Stateless services cannot contain bugs that affect what their users see in any way

questions.explanation: If a stateless service has a bug, you can fix it and restart, and everything returns to normal. Stateful systems are designed to remember things more or less forever, so if a bug writes bad data, its effects can also last forever. Transactions (atomicity, isolation, durability) have been the main tool for correctness for about four decades, but those foundations are weaker than they seem, as the confusion around weak isolation levels shows.

questions.question: How reliable are current engineering methods for determining whether an application is safe to run at a particular isolation level or replication configuration?

options.text: Surprisingly flaky: simple approaches seem fine at low concurrency but hide bugs
Dependable: vendors' documented isolation guarantees match behaviour under faults
Mature: routine load testing reliably exposes any isolation or replication anomaly
Adequate: anomalies arise only from misconfiguration, which tooling now catches

questions.explanation: It is very difficult to determine whether an application is safe at a given isolation level or replication configuration: our understanding and engineering methods here are surprisingly flaky. Simple solutions often appear to work when concurrency is low and there are no faults, but have subtle bugs under more demanding conditions, which is why ordinary load testing does not reliably expose them. Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen experiments have shown stark gaps between some products' documented safety guarantees and their actual behaviour under network problems and crashes, and even with correct infrastructure, application code must still use hard-to-understand features (weak isolation, quorum settings) correctly.

questions.question: If an application needs strong assurances of correctness, serializability and atomic commit are established approaches. What cost do they typically carry?

options.text: They typically work only within one datacenter and limit scale and fault tolerance
They scale freely across regions, because commit latency does not depend on distance
They mainly cost CPU, so adding cores removes the limits on scale and fault tolerance
They require the whole dataset to fit in one node's memory, ruling out partitioning

questions.explanation: Serializability and atomic commit give strong guarantees but rely on coordination: commits must wait for round trips between participants, so latency grows with distance and any unavailable participant blocks progress. As a result they typically work only in a single datacenter (ruling out geographically distributed architectures) and limit the scale and fault tolerance you can achieve; the limit comes from coordination, not from CPU or from needing the data in one node's memory. The traditional transaction approach is not going away, but it is not the last word on building correct, fault-resilient applications; dataflow architectures offer other ways to think about correctness.

questions.question: What is the core thesis of the end-to-end argument as applied to databases?

options.text: Strong guarantees such as serializability do not alone prevent data loss or corruption
Serializable transactions guarantee that an application is free of any data corruption
Making all data immutable is sufficient on its own to solve every correctness problem
Application bugs that corrupt data are rare enough in practice to be safely ignored

questions.explanation: Using a data system with strong safety properties, such as serializable transactions, does not mean the application is free from data loss or corruption. If application code writes incorrect data or deletes data, serializable transactions will not help, and if a user's request is retried across a network failure it may be executed twice. Immutable, append-only data makes recovery from such mistakes easier but is not a cure-all; the application itself must take end-to-end measures, such as duplicate suppression.

questions.question: When something goes wrong while processing a message, what are the two basic choices, and what risk does each carry?

options.text: Drop it and lose data, or retry and risk processing it twice
Retry and guarantee it is processed once, or drop it and lose nothing
Roll it back with two-phase commit, or skip it without any data loss
Delay it until clocks synchronize, or reorder it by its timestamp

questions.explanation: If processing fails you can give up, dropping the message and incurring data loss, or try again. Retrying risks duplicate processing, because the first attempt may actually have succeeded without you finding out, and processing twice is itself data corruption (charging a customer twice, or double-counting a metric). Exactly-once semantics means arranging the computation so the final effect is as if no fault occurred, even though the operation was retried; making the operation idempotent is one of the most effective ways, which may require tracking operation IDs and fencing during failover.

questions.question: What does TCP use packet sequence numbers for, and what limits the scope of its duplicate suppression?

options.text: Ordering packets and detecting loss or duplicates, only within one connection
Ordering packets across every connection between the same two hosts, even after reconnects
Deduplicating application requests for the lifetime of the client process
Only congestion control; packet duplicates are left to the application

questions.explanation: TCP uses sequence numbers to put packets in the right order at the recipient and to detect lost or duplicated packets; it retransmits lost ones and discards duplicates before handing data to the application. But this works only within one connection. Many databases tie a transaction to a client connection, so if the connection times out after the client sends COMMIT, the client does not know whether the transaction committed, and a retry on a new connection is outside TCP's duplicate suppression.

questions.question: A client asks to transfer $11; the database commits, but the acknowledgment is lost and the client retries. What is the failure window and resulting duplicate effect?

options.text: The commit was sent but not acknowledged, so a retry can transfer $22 in total
TCP duplicate suppression discards the retried transaction on the new connection
The database recognizes the retry as a duplicate and ignores it automatically
The retry is harmless because adding and subtracting a fixed amount is idempotent

questions.explanation: The transaction does balance = balance + 11.00 on one account and balance - 11.00 on another. If the network fails after the client sends COMMIT but before it hears the outcome, the client cannot tell whether the transfer committed. Retrying on a new connection is outside TCP's duplicate suppression, and the database sees an ordinary new transaction, so if the first attempt did commit, 2 x $11 = $22 moves. The statements are not idempotent; real banks do not work this way.

questions.question: A committed money transfer is retried because the end-user never received an acknowledgment. Does two-phase commit prevent this end-to-end duplicate, and why?

options.text: No: it lets a coordinator resolve in-doubt transactions, but not the end-user's retries
Yes: two-phase commit deduplicates any retried request all the way from end to end
Yes: two-phase commit ties each transaction to one TCP connection, rejecting retries
No: two-phase commit itself commits each in-doubt transaction twice during recovery

questions.explanation: Two-phase commit breaks the one-to-one mapping between a TCP connection and a transaction, because the coordinator must be able to reconnect to a database after a network fault and tell it to commit or abort an in-doubt transaction. That helps between the database client and server, but not between the end-user device and the application server: if a browser's POST times out and the user resubmits, the web server sees a separate request and the database a separate transaction.

questions.question: A browser may resubmit a form's POST request after a timeout. What makes the operation idempotent across all network hops from the end-user client to the database?

options.text: A client-generated operation ID, checked for uniqueness at the database
A stronger transaction isolation level, such as serializable, configured in the database
A longer TCP timeout on the client's connection, so that responses are less often lost
The Post/Redirect/Get pattern applied on the web server after every form submission

questions.explanation: Database transactions alone are not enough; you must consider the end-to-end flow of the request. Generate a unique ID for the operation (a UUID in a hidden form field, or a hash of the relevant form fields), so a resubmitted POST carries the same ID, and pass it all the way to the database. Inserting it into a requests table with a uniqueness constraint makes a duplicate INSERT fail and abort its transaction. Post/Redirect/Get avoids the browser's resubmit warning in normal operation but does not help when the POST times out.

questions.question: A client-generated request ID is inserted into a uniqueness-constrained requests table to deduplicate retries. Besides deduplication, what role does this table play?

options.text: A kind of event log, pointing toward event sourcing
A cache of the most recent account balances
A secondary index over the accounts table
A lock table that serializes all transfers

questions.explanation: Besides suppressing duplicates, the requests table records each accepted request as a fact, which makes it a kind of event log. The balance updates need not happen in the same transaction as inserting the request: they are redundant and could be derived from the request event by a downstream consumer, as long as each event is processed exactly once, which the same request ID can enforce. That is the basic event-sourcing pattern.

questions.question: Who articulated the end-to-end argument in system design, and in what year?

options.text: Saltzer, Reed, and Clark, in 1984
Leslie Lamport, in 1978
Jim Gray, in 1981
Eric Brewer, in 2000

questions.explanation: Saltzer, Reed, and Clark stated in 1984 that a function such as duplicate suppression can be implemented completely and correctly only with the knowledge and help of the application at the endpoints of the communication system; an incomplete version in the communication system may still be useful as a performance enhancement. TCP suppresses duplicate packets and some stream processors offer exactly-once message processing, but only a transaction identifier passed from the end-user client to the database can rule out duplicate user requests.

questions.question: Applying the end-to-end argument to data integrity and encryption, which statements hold? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Link and transport checksums cannot detect endpoint or disk corruption
Wi-Fi and TLS cannot protect data after a server compromise; end-to-end encryption can
Lower-layer protections remain useful because they reduce higher-level failures
Checksums at one lower layer are sufficient for end-to-end integrity
