questions.explanation: Ethernet, TCP, and TLS checksums detect packet corruption in the network, but not corruption from software bugs at either end or on the disks where data is stored, so end-to-end checksums are needed. Similarly, Wi-Fi passwords protect only the local link and TLS only the network path, not a compromised server; only end-to-end encryption and authentication cover all of these. Low-level features are still useful because they reduce the probability of higher-level problems, but they are not sufficient by themselves.

optionExplanations.a: A transport checksum covers corruption only along that hop; it cannot detect bad memory, disk errors, or application bugs at the endpoints. End-to-end validation must cover the whole path.
optionExplanations.b: Wi-Fi and TLS encrypt particular links, but a compromised server sees plaintext after decryption. End-to-end encryption keeps intermediaries from becoming trusted plaintext endpoints.
optionExplanations.c: Lower-layer checks still prevent many faults cheaply and reduce the burden on end-to-end mechanisms. The argument says they are insufficient alone, not useless.
optionExplanations.d: A checksum at one layer leaves corruption before that layer's input or after its output undetected. Passing a hop-level check is not proof of complete end-to-end integrity.

questions.question: Low-level mechanisms (TCP, database transactions, stream processors) cannot by themselves guarantee end-to-end correctness, so applications must add measures such as end-to-end duplicate suppression. Why is this regrettable?

options.text: Fault-tolerance mechanisms are hard to get right, and no good abstraction yet hides them
The end-to-end argument has since been shown to be incorrect for modern networks
Low-level mechanisms such as TCP work too poorly to be worth using in the first place
Transactions already offer a complete abstraction for this, which applications ignore

questions.explanation: Low-level reliability mechanisms work quite well, so the remaining higher-level faults are rare, and it would be nice to wrap the remaining fault-tolerance machinery in an abstraction so application code need not worry about it. Transactions collapse many problems into commit or abort, a huge simplification, but are not enough and are expensive across heterogeneous systems. Avoiding them pushes fault tolerance into application code, and since concurrency and partial failure are hard to reason about, most such mechanisms probably do not work correctly, leading to lost or corrupted data.

questions.question: What kind of fault-tolerance abstraction is worth exploring for large-scale distributed data systems?

options.text: One that makes application-specific end-to-end correctness easy and performs well at scale
Abandoning fault tolerance entirely in favour of fast automatic restarts after each failure
Returning to single-node systems wherever that is at all possible, to avoid partial failure
Standardizing the whole industry on XA distributed transactions across all data systems

questions.explanation: The desired abstraction combines three things: it makes it easy to provide application-specific end-to-end correctness properties, and it maintains good performance and good operational characteristics in a large-scale distributed environment. Distributed transactions are too expensive across heterogeneous technologies, and hand-written application-level fault tolerance is usually wrong, so neither existing extreme is satisfactory.

questions.question: Which constraints involve concurrent conflicting operations that must be decided at a single point, as a uniqueness constraint does? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A username must uniquely identify one user
An account balance must never go negative
Items sold must not exceed the stock in the warehouse
A user's biography must be under 500 characters

questions.explanation: Uniqueness constraints (usernames, email addresses, file names, seat bookings) and similar constraints (non-negative balances, no overselling stock, non-overlapping room bookings) all involve concurrent requests that compete for one scarce resource, so the system must decide which succeed and reject the rest. Techniques for enforcing uniqueness often apply to these too. A length limit, by contrast, can be checked on each value in isolation.

optionExplanations.a: Two concurrent registrations of the same username conflict, so all claims for that name must reach one decision point that accepts exactly one and rejects the other.
optionExplanations.b: Two concurrent withdrawals might each be fine alone but together overdraw the account, so debits on the same account must be validated against one authoritative balance.
optionExplanations.c: Concurrent orders checked against a stale stock count could together exceed inventory, so decrements for the same item need a single point of validation.
optionExplanations.d: A length limit depends only on the value being written, not on any competing operation, so each write can be validated independently with no coordination.

questions.question: Why does a uniqueness constraint require consensus?

options.text: The system must decide which of several concurrent conflicting requests is accepted
Every node must hold a complete copy of the data to check for duplicates
Uniqueness checks must compare synchronized physical clock timestamps
Consensus is needed simply to make each individual write durable on disk

questions.explanation: If several requests concurrently claim the same value, the system must decide which one is accepted and reject the others, which is a consensus problem. The usual approach is a single leader for each value that makes the decisions; uniqueness checking can scale by partitioning on the unique value (for example by hash of username), but tolerating leader failure brings back consensus. Asynchronous multi-leader replication is ruled out, because different leaders could accept conflicting writes concurrently.

questions.question: When log-based messaging is used to enforce a uniqueness constraint, what guarantee does the log provide, and what lets a stream processor decide unambiguously which conflicting request came first?

options.text: Total order broadcast within a partition, consumed sequentially by a single thread
At-least-once delivery, with a distributed lock choosing the winning request
Durability only, with synchronized physical clocks choosing the winner
Exactly-once delivery, with each client choosing the winner itself

questions.explanation: A log ensures all consumers see messages in the same order, which is total order broadcast and equivalent to consensus. A stream processor consumes one log partition sequentially on a single thread, so if the log is partitioned by the value that must be unique, the processor sees all conflicting requests in one deterministic order and can decide which came first. This mirrors implementing linearizable storage using total order broadcast.

questions.question: Which steps belong to the log-based algorithm for enforcing unique usernames? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Hash each username request into a partitioned log
Process each partition serially and emit success or rejection
Have the client await the matching result event
Acquire a global lock before appending each request

questions.explanation: Each username request is appended to a log partition chosen by the hash of the username. A stream processor reads each partition sequentially, using a local database to track taken names, and emits a success or rejection message to an output stream. The requesting client waits for the message for its request. The method scales by adding partitions, and works for other constraints too: any writes that may conflict are routed to the same partition and processed sequentially, with arbitrary validation logic.

optionExplanations.a: Hashing by username routes every potentially conflicting claim for that name to one log partition. Different names can still scale across partitions independently.
optionExplanations.b: One serial processor per partition evaluates claims in log order and emits a deterministic accept or reject result. This is the point where the uniqueness constraint is enforced.
optionExplanations.c: The client waits for the result carrying its request identity so it knows whether its durable proposal succeeded. Append acknowledgement alone would not reveal constraint outcome.
optionExplanations.d: A global lock would serialize unrelated usernames and destroy partitioned scalability. Per-key routing already provides the necessary conflict boundary.

questions.question: A money transfer touches three partitions: one holding the request ID, one the payer's account, and one the payee's. What does the traditional database approach require, and with what consequence?

options.text: Atomic commit across all three, coupling them in one total order and lowering throughput
A single-partition write, because the three items are always stored in the same partition
Asynchronous replication between the three partitions, with no coordination needed at all
A uniqueness check on the request ID alone, with no cross-partition step for the accounts

questions.explanation: There is no reason the request ID, payer account, and payee account should live in the same partition. Traditionally, executing the transaction would need an atomic commit across all three partitions, which effectively forces it into a total order with every other transaction on any of those partitions. Since there is now cross-partition coordination, the partitions can no longer be processed independently and throughput is likely to suffer.

questions.question: Which steps achieve a correct multi-partition money transfer without an atomic commit protocol? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Append one request-ID-tagged transfer request to the log
Derive debit and credit instructions partitioned by their accounts
Deduplicate each instruction by request ID before changing balances
Run two-phase commit across the request and account partitions

questions.explanation: The client gives the transfer a unique request ID and appends it as one message to a log partition chosen by that ID; single-object writes are atomic, so the request either is in the log or is not. A stream processor reads the requests and emits a debit instruction partitioned by the payer and a credit instruction partitioned by the payee, both carrying the request ID. Further processors deduplicate by request ID and apply the changes. If the client sent debit and credit directly, an atomic commit across two partitions would be needed.

optionExplanations.a: Writing one request message atomically creates a durable source of truth for the transfer. Either that request exists or it does not, avoiding a half-issued debit and credit.
optionExplanations.b: Deterministic consumers derive separate debit and credit instructions and route each to its account partition. Both effects originate from the same immutable request.
optionExplanations.c: The request ID lets each account partition recognize a replayed instruction and avoid applying it twice. Deduplication turns retry into safe recovery.
optionExplanations.d: Two-phase commit is the mechanism this log-derived design is intended to avoid. A single durable request plus idempotent derivations supplies integrity without locking all partitions together.

questions.question: A stream processor reads each transfer request and emits debit and credit instructions carrying the same request ID. If that processor crashes and replays output, why is duplication harmless?

options.text: Being deterministic, it re-emits identical instructions, deduplicated by request ID
The crash discards every instruction emitted before the processor restarted
Checkpointing guarantees that no request message is ever processed twice, even after a crash
Downstream consumers deduplicate instructions by their arrival timestamps

questions.explanation: After a crash, the processor resumes from its last checkpoint, so it skips no requests but may process some again and emit duplicate debit and credit instructions. Because it is deterministic, the duplicates are identical, and the downstream account processors deduplicate them using the end-to-end request ID. The result is that every request is applied exactly once to both accounts without atomic commit. An extra processor partitioned by payer can also validate balances before requests enter the log, to prevent overdrafts.

questions.question: What convenient property do transactions typically have that a pipeline of asynchronous stream-processing stages lacks?

options.text: Linearizability: once committed, writes are visible to all readers
Durability: once acknowledged, a write survives crashes of the system
Ordering: writes within one partition are processed in a fixed sequence
Determinism: replaying the same input reproduces the same derived state

questions.explanation: A transaction is typically linearizable: the writer waits until it commits, and thereafter its writes are visible to all readers. Log consumers are asynchronous by design, so a sender does not wait for its message to be processed. A client can still choose to wait for the result on an output stream, as in log-based uniqueness checking, but the correctness of the check does not depend on that waiting. Durability, per-partition ordering, and deterministic replay are all available in log-based pipelines.

questions.question: The term 'consistency' conflates two different requirements, timeliness and integrity. What does each mean?

options.text: Timeliness is being up to date; integrity is absence of corruption
Timeliness means absence of corruption and integrity means up-to-dateness
Timeliness concerns read latency, and integrity concerns write latency
Timeliness concerns durability and integrity concerns availability

questions.explanation: Timeliness means users observe the system in an up-to-date state; reading a stale replica violates it only temporarily, since waiting and retrying resolves it. Linearizability (as in CAP) is a strong form of timeliness and read-after-write consistency a weaker one. Integrity means absence of corruption: no data loss and no contradictory or false data, for example an index must correctly reflect the database. Integrity violations are permanent and need explicit checking and repair; ACID consistency is essentially an application-specific notion of integrity.

questions.question: In slogan form, how are violations of timeliness and violations of integrity characterized?

options.text: Timeliness violations are 'eventual consistency'; integrity violations are 'perpetual inconsistency'
Integrity violations are 'eventual consistency'; timeliness violations are 'perpetual inconsistency'
Each kind is a form of 'eventual consistency', differing only in how long it lasts
Each kind is a form of 'perpetual inconsistency', requiring explicit repair to fix

questions.explanation: A timeliness violation fixes itself once updates propagate, which is what eventual consistency describes; an integrity violation persists until someone explicitly detects and repairs it. In most applications integrity matters much more. On a credit card statement, a transaction from the last 24 hours not yet appearing is normal lag; a balance that does not equal previous balance plus transactions, or a charge never paid to the merchant, would be a serious integrity violation.

questions.question: Why is the distinction between timeliness and integrity fairly inconsequential when reasoning in terms of ACID transactions?

options.text: ACID transactions usually provide both timeliness (linearizability) and integrity
ACID transactions provide neither timeliness nor integrity guarantees to applications
ACID transactions provide timeliness but leave integrity entirely to the application
ACID transactions provide integrity but are never linearizable for any of their readers

questions.explanation: Because ACID transactions usually give both guarantees together, someone approaching correctness from that viewpoint rarely needs to separate them. Event-based dataflow systems decouple the two: asynchronous processing gives no timeliness guarantee unless consumers explicitly wait, but integrity is central, preserved by exactly-once or effectively-once semantics, fault-tolerant delivery, and duplicate suppression. That decoupling is what lets them achieve comparable correctness with better performance and robustness.

questions.question: Which mechanisms let reliable stream processing preserve integrity without distributed transactions or atomic commit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Representing the whole write operation as one message that can be written atomically
Deriving all other state updates from that message with deterministic functions
Passing a client-generated request ID through every stage for duplicate suppression
Holding a distributed lock across all affected partitions during the write

questions.explanation: Integrity is achieved by combining several mechanisms: capture the write as a single atomically written message (a good fit for event sourcing); derive all other state updates from it with deterministic derivation functions, like stored procedures; pass a client-generated request ID through every level to enable end-to-end duplicate suppression; and keep messages immutable so derived data can be reprocessed to recover from bugs. None of these requires locking all partitions together.

optionExplanations.a: A single message can be appended atomically, so the operation either exists in the log or does not; there is no half-written multi-partition state to recover from.
optionExplanations.b: Deterministic derivation means a replay after a crash produces exactly the same downstream updates, so recovery can safely reprocess the message instead of guessing what partially happened.
optionExplanations.c: A stable request ID lets every downstream stage recognize and drop repeated instructions, which closes the retry gaps that TCP or per-stage exactly-once processing alone would leave.
optionExplanations.d: A distributed lock across partitions reintroduces synchronous cross-partition coordination, the cost this design is meant to avoid; integrity comes from durable messages and idempotent derivation instead.

questions.question: Which limitation is unavoidable if an application wants a traditional, strict uniqueness constraint?

options.text: It requires consensus, typically by funneling all events for a partition through one node
It cannot be implemented at all in any distributed system
It can be enforced with asynchronous multi-leader replication and no coordination
It requires a single global lock covering every partition of the database

questions.explanation: Enforcing a strict uniqueness constraint requires consensus, usually implemented by routing all events in a partition through a single node; stream processing cannot avoid this either. It is still achievable and scalable via partitioning, so neither impossibility nor a global lock is required. What many applications can do instead is accept a weaker notion of uniqueness: if two people register the same username concurrently, apologize to one and ask them to choose another, which is a compensating transaction.

questions.question: Customers order more items than a warehouse holds. Why might a linearizable stock-count constraint be unnecessary, by comparison with a forklift truck damaging stock?

options.text: An apology workflow (restock, apologize, discount) is needed for damage anyway
A linearizable count stops overselling, so damage handling can be skipped entirely
Forklift damage is rare, so the stock count is accurate enough without any checks
Overselling can only be fixed by refunds, which cost more than enforcing the constraint

questions.explanation: If you oversell, you can order more stock, apologize for the delay, and offer a discount. That is exactly what you would have to do anyway if a forklift truck ran over some items and left you with less stock than you thought: a linearizable stock count cannot prevent physical damage, so the shortfall-handling workflow must exist regardless. Since it exists, it can also absorb occasional overselling, so requiring a linearizable constraint on the stock count may be unnecessary. Airlines and hotels likewise overbook deliberately and handle the excess with compensation processes.

questions.question: How can a bank handle a customer withdrawing more money than their balance without enforcing a strict, synchronous constraint?

options.text: Charge a fee, require repayment, and cap risk with daily withdrawal limits
Reject every withdrawal until all replicas have agreed on the current balance
Allow unlimited overdrafts, since a later apology always fully repairs the loss
Automatically reclaim the ATM cash payout once the overdraft is detected

questions.explanation: The bank can treat the violation as something to fix afterwards: charge an overdraft fee, ask the customer to pay back what they owe, and limit total withdrawals per day so its risk is bounded. Whether the cost of such an apology is acceptable is a business decision. Cash already paid out of an ATM cannot be directly taken back, which is why validation should still happen before actions that are expensive to recover from, even if it need not happen before every write.

questions.question: Applications such as overbooking or overdraft handling can repair constraint violations through compensation. Do they need timely constraint checking, integrity, or both?

options.text: Integrity, but not timeliness of the constraint check
Timeliness of the check, while integrity can be relaxed
Both, with the constraint enforced before every write
Only availability, since compensation can repair any problem later

questions.explanation: These applications still need integrity: no lost reservations, and no money disappearing through mismatched credits and debits. But they do not need timeliness in enforcing the constraint: if more items were sold than are in stock, the problem can be patched up afterwards by apologizing or compensating. So the system can write optimistically and check the constraint after the fact, similar to conflict resolution in multi-leader replication.

questions.question: Which two observations together support coordination-avoiding data systems?

options.text: Dataflow keeps integrity without atomic commit, and many apps tolerate loose constraints
Dataflow systems need atomic commit, and every application needs strictly enforced constraints
Dataflow systems cannot maintain integrity, but most applications turn out not to need it
Coordination is unavoidable, so every constraint must be checked synchronously before writing

questions.explanation: First, dataflow systems can maintain integrity on derived data without atomic commit, linearizability, or synchronous cross-partition coordination. Second, strict uniqueness needs timeliness and coordination, but many applications are fine with constraints that are temporarily violated and fixed later, as long as integrity holds. Together these allow systems with strong integrity and better performance and fault tolerance, for example multi-leader across datacenters with weak timeliness. Serializable transactions can still be used at small scope, and coordination can be added only where recovery would be impossible.

questions.question: How can coordination and strict constraints be viewed in terms of the apologies a business must make?

options.text: They reduce apologies for inconsistencies but may increase apologies for outages
They eliminate the need for any kind of apology, whether for inconsistency or outage
They reduce apologies for inconsistencies and for outages at the same time
They increase apologies for inconsistencies while reducing apologies for outages

questions.explanation: Coordination and constraints reduce the number of apologies needed for inconsistencies, but they can also reduce performance and availability, potentially increasing apologies for outages. You cannot get the number of apologies to zero; the aim is the sweet spot with neither too many inconsistencies nor too many availability problems for your needs.

questions.question: In reasoning about correctness and fault tolerance, what is a system model?

options.text: Assumptions about which faults can occur and which cannot
A performance model that predicts a system's throughput and latency under load
The deployment topology of the system's nodes, racks, and datacenters
The data model (relational, document, or graph) that the system exposes

questions.explanation: A system model states what we assume can go wrong (processes crash, machines lose power, networks delay or drop messages) and what cannot (data survives fsync, memory is not corrupted, the CPU multiplies correctly). Traditional models treat this as binary, but in reality it is a matter of probabilities: the question is whether violations of the assumptions happen often enough to be encountered in practice, as large fleets make rare events likely.

questions.question: What evidence suggests that random memory corruption is not merely theoretical, and how common is it?

options.text: Crash reports explainable only by bit-flips, plus rowhammer; still very rare today
Bit-flips are common and happen constantly on every running machine in a fleet
Bit-flips cannot occur at all on modern hardware equipped with error correction
Bit-flips have only ever been observed in controlled laboratory experiments

questions.explanation: An application collecting crash reports from many client devices received some that could only be explained by random bit-flips in device memory: with enough devices, very unlikely things happen. Besides hardware faults or radiation, certain pathological memory access patterns can flip bits even in fault-free memory (rowhammer), which can be used to break operating-system security. Random bit-flips remain very rare on modern hardware, but not impossible, so they deserve some attention.

questions.question: Which bugs in mature, widely used relational databases illustrate that even battle-tested database software can fail to preserve integrity?

options.text: MySQL violating a uniqueness constraint; PostgreSQL serializable allowing write skew
MySQL and PostgreSQL aborting deadlocked transactions under heavy concurrent load
None: mature relational databases have proved free of integrity bugs of this kind
Only bugs in young NoSQL stores, which mature relational databases have always avoided

questions.explanation: Cases have been seen of MySQL failing to correctly maintain a uniqueness constraint and of PostgreSQL's serializable isolation level exhibiting write skew, despite both being robust, well-regarded databases battle-tested for many years. Aborting deadlocked transactions, by contrast, is normal concurrency control: the transaction is rolled back and can be retried, so integrity is preserved. Application code receives far less review and testing, so it has many more bugs, and many applications do not even use database integrity features such as foreign keys or uniqueness constraints correctly. ACID consistency assumes transactions are bug-free; if the application misuses the database, for example using weak isolation unsafely, integrity cannot be guaranteed.

questions.question: What is auditing in data systems, and is it relevant only to financial applications?

options.text: Checking the integrity of data; valuable beyond finance, which relies on it most
Checking the integrity of data; relevant only to financial applications and banks
Logging every query that is issued against the database; relevant to all applications
An unnecessary activity for any application that uses ACID transactions throughout

questions.explanation: Since hardware and software do not always live up to their promises, data corruption is inevitable sooner or later, so we need a way to find out whether data has been corrupted, fix it, and trace the source; checking integrity is called auditing. Auditability is especially important in finance because everyone knows mistakes happen, but the same reasoning applies to any data that matters. ACID transactions do not remove the need, because bugs and hardware faults occur below and above them.

questions.question: Large-scale storage systems such as HDFS and Amazon S3 run background processes that read back files, compare replicas, and move data between disks. What assumption about disks underlies this design?

options.text: Disks work correctly most of the time, but not always
Disks always work correctly once data has been fsynced
Disks never work reliably, so every read must be repeated
Disk errors are always reported promptly by the hardware

questions.explanation: HDFS and S3 do not fully trust disks: they continually read back and verify data to mitigate the risk of silent corruption. That still assumes disks usually work, which is reasonable, but is different from assuming they always work. The same 'trust, but verify' logic says you must actually read data to know it is still there, and should test restoring backups regularly, rather than discovering a broken backup after data is lost.

questions.question: Why is a transaction that mutates several objects in a database hard to audit after the fact, compared with an event-sourced system?

options.text: The mutations don't show why they were made; event sourcing keeps the input as one event
Event-sourced systems are harder to audit, because they discard the input behind each change
Neither approach records enough information to audit anything after the fact
Both approaches record the intent behind each change equally well in their logs

questions.explanation: Even with captured transaction logs, insertions, updates, and deletions across tables do not necessarily show why they were performed, and the application logic that decided on them was transient and cannot be reproduced. In event sourcing, user input is a single immutable event and all resulting state updates are derived from it deterministically, so rerunning the same events through the same code reproduces the same state. That makes provenance clear and enables integrity checks: hash the event log, rerun derivations, and debug by replaying exact circumstances.

questions.question: Why is checking the integrity of data systems best done end to end?

options.text: A check spanning more systems leaves fewer places for corruption to hide
Per-component checks together already cover everything an end-to-end check would
End-to-end checks are specifically mandated by data-protection law
End-to-end checks remove the need for any lower-level checksums

questions.explanation: If no individual component can be fully trusted to be free of hardware faults or bugs, data must be checked periodically. Checks on each component miss corruption that happens between components or in the glue code, whereas checking an entire derived-data pipeline end to end implicitly covers every disk, network, service, and algorithm along the path. Continuous end-to-end checks, like automated tests, catch bugs quickly and give confidence to change the system. Lower-level checksums remain useful for reducing problems, but are not sufficient on their own.

questions.question: What is the current state of tooling for auditable data systems?

options.text: Few systems make it top-level; some apps keep audit tables whose integrity is hard to guarantee
Most data systems already make auditability a top-level design concern for their users
Signing the transaction log with a hardware security module guarantees the right transactions went in
Audit tables automatically stay consistent with the database state that they describe

questions.explanation: Not many data systems make auditability a top-level concern. Some applications log all changes to a separate audit table, but guaranteeing the integrity of both the audit log and the database is still difficult. Periodically signing a transaction log with a hardware security module makes it tamper-proof, but does not prove the right transactions went into it. Cryptographic tools such as Merkle trees (used in blockchains and certificate transparency) offer interesting integrity-checking ideas, though proof-of-work is wasteful and scalability needs work.

questions.question: In considering the ethics of building data systems, what should engineers keep in mind about the datasets they work with?

options.text: Many datasets are about people, who must be treated with humanity and respect
Data is an abstract resource whose meaning is purely technical
Ethical consequences are the concern of legal teams, not engineers
A technology's effects are fixed by the technology, not by how it is used

questions.explanation: Every system is built for a purpose, and every action has intended and unintended consequences that may reach far beyond that purpose. Engineers therefore have a responsibility to consider those consequences. Although data is discussed abstractly, many datasets describe people's behaviour, interests, and identity, and human dignity is paramount. A technology is not good or bad in itself; what matters is how it is used and how it affects people, which is why the ethical responsibility cannot be handed off.

questions.question: Which ethical guideline exists specifically to help software engineers navigate ethical choices, and how much is it used?

options.text: The ACM Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice, rarely applied
The IEEE code of ethics, which is rigorously enforced for all practising software engineers
None: no ethical guidelines for software engineers have ever been written down
The GDPR, which serves as the software profession's binding code of ethics

questions.explanation: Guidelines such as the ACM's Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice exist, but they are rarely discussed, applied, or enforced. As a result, engineers and product managers sometimes take a very cavalier attitude toward privacy and the potential negative consequences of their products. The GDPR is a data-protection law, not a professional ethics code.

questions.question: Within predictive analytics, which distinction matters most ethically?

options.text: Predicting weather or disease spread, versus predicting individuals' behaviour
Supervised learning methods, versus unsupervised learning methods
Batch prediction over stored data, versus streaming prediction over live events
Simple linear models, versus complex nonlinear models such as deep networks

questions.explanation: Predicting the weather or the spread of diseases is one thing; predicting whether a convict will reoffend, a loan applicant will default, or an insurance customer will make expensive claims directly affects individual lives. Organizations naturally want to be cautious, since a missed opportunity costs them little while a bad loan or hire costs much, so if in doubt they say no; for the people labeled risky, those 'no' decisions accumulate. The modelling technique matters far less than whom the predictions are about.

questions.question: What is an 'algorithmic prison'?

options.text: Systematic exclusion from jobs, travel, insurance, and loans after a risky label
Software engineers being held legally liable for every one of their algorithms' errors
Being locked into one platform because personal data cannot be exported elsewhere
A sentencing algorithm that directly decides the length of convicted people's prison terms

questions.explanation: Someone accurately or falsely labeled as risky by algorithms may face many 'no' decisions across jobs, air travel, insurance, rental housing, and financial services. That is such a large constraint on freedom that it has been called 'algorithmic prison'. Unlike a justice system that presumes innocence until proven guilty, automated systems can systematically and arbitrarily exclude a person from society without proof of guilt and with little chance of appeal.

questions.question: Beyond automating a human's decision with explicit software rules, what further step do predictive analytics systems take?

options.text: They infer the decision rules themselves from data, producing opaque patterns
They make the decision rules explicit so that they can be easily audited by anyone
They automatically remove any bias that is present in their input training data
They require a human to approve each learned rule before it is used in decisions

questions.explanation: Predictive analytics leaves the rules for saying yes or no to be inferred from data, and the learned patterns are opaque: even if there is a correlation, we may not know why. If the input contains systematic bias, the system will most likely learn and amplify it. Removing protected traits does not help when other features are correlated with them, for example postal code or IP address predicting race in segregated neighbourhoods, which is why machine learning has been satirized as 'money laundering for bias'.

questions.question: What do predictive analytics systems do to the past?

options.text: They extrapolate from the past, so a discriminatory past gets codified
They correct historical bias automatically, so data should lead decisions
They model causal mechanisms, so correlations with protected traits vanish
They treat each person independently, without reference to others' behaviour

questions.explanation: Predictive models extrapolate from historical data; if that past was discriminatory, they codify the discrimination. Making the future better than the past requires moral imagination, which only humans can provide, so data and models should be tools, not masters. Such models typically rely on correlations rather than causes, and they work by comparing a person with similar people, not by assessing each individual in isolation.

questions.question: Which are genuine open questions raised by automated decision-making about people? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Who is accountable when an algorithm's decision is wrong, and how affected people can appeal
Who is responsible when a self-driving car causes an accident
What recourse exists if a credit-scoring algorithm systematically discriminates by race or religion
Whether publishing a model's source code by itself discharges accountability for its decisions

questions.explanation: When a human makes a mistake they can be held accountable and the affected person can appeal; algorithms make mistakes too, but it is unclear who is accountable. Similar questions arise for self-driving car accidents, discriminatory credit scoring, and explaining a model's decision under judicial review. Making algorithms accountable and transparent is an unsolved problem, but publishing code alone does not make decisions explainable or fair.

optionExplanations.a: Automated decisions still make mistakes, but there is no obvious person to hold accountable and often no route for appeal, unlike decisions made by a human.
optionExplanations.b: A self-driving car's accident may involve designers, manufacturers, operators, and data providers, so assigning responsibility is genuinely unresolved rather than obvious.
optionExplanations.c: Discrimination hidden inside learned scoring logic can be hard to detect or contest, so whether affected groups have any recourse is a real open question.
optionExplanations.d: Publishing source code does not reveal training-data bias, explain individual decisions, or create an appeal path, so code release clearly does not by itself settle accountability; this is a misconception, not an open question.

questions.question: Why is a traditional credit score usually more contestable than an opaque machine-learning risk score?

options.text: It uses relevant borrowing-history facts, and errors in them can be corrected
It is opaque, whereas machine-learning scores are transparent and explainable
It cannot be corrected, whereas machine-learning scores can be easily corrected
It relies on the same wide inputs, so both are equally easy to contest

questions.explanation: A credit score is normally based on relevant facts about a person's actual borrowing history, and errors in the record can be corrected, although agencies do not make this easy. Machine-learning scoring uses a much wider range of inputs and is more opaque, making it hard to see how a decision came about. A credit score asks 'how did you behave in the past?', whereas predictive analytics asks 'who is similar to you, and how did people like you behave?', which amounts to stereotyping and leaves little recourse for erroneous data.

questions.question: Average life expectancy in a country is 80 years, yet that says little about when any particular person will die. What does this illustrate about decisions based on statistical predictions?

options.text: A correct overall distribution says little about one person's outcome
Each individual can be expected to live to almost exactly 80 years of age
A correct overall distribution guarantees accurate predictions for each individual
Statistical data cannot be used to make any kind of useful prediction at all

questions.explanation: An average life expectancy of 80 does not mean you are expected to die on your 80th birthday; from the average and distribution you can say little about the age to which one person will live. Likewise, a prediction system's output is probabilistic and may well be wrong in individual cases even if it is right on average. Blind belief in the supremacy of data for decisions is therefore dangerous, and we must make algorithms accountable and fix their inevitable mistakes.

questions.question: Analytics can reveal financial and social characteristics of people's lives. How can this cut both ways?

options.text: It can target aid to those in need, or help predatory firms find vulnerable people
It can only ever be used for good, since more knowledge about people helps everyone
It can only ever be used for harm, so such analytics should be banned outright
It reveals only aggregate population trends, never any individual's circumstances

questions.explanation: The same analytic power that identifies people in financial or social difficulty could be used to direct aid and support to them. It is also sometimes used by predatory businesses to find vulnerable people and sell them risky products such as high-cost loans and worthless college degrees. The challenge is to prevent data being used to harm people while realizing its positive potential.

questions.question: Employers use credit scores to evaluate job applicants. A good worker suffers a misfortune and starts missing bill payments. What feedback loop can follow?

options.text: The score drops, jobs get harder to find, and joblessness lowers it further
The score rises with job tenure, improving the person's prospects in a virtuous cycle
Employers disregard the drop in the score once the person has been reemployed
The loop corrects itself, because credit scores reset after each new job is found

questions.explanation: Missed payments lower the credit score, which makes finding work harder; joblessness pushes the person toward poverty, which worsens the score further, making employment even harder. This downward spiral is hidden behind a camouflage of mathematical rigor. Such feedback loops cannot always be predicted, but many consequences can be anticipated through systems thinking: considering the whole system including the people interacting with it, and asking whether it amplifies existing differences or combats injustice.

questions.question: How does a system's relationship with a user differ between storing data the user explicitly entered and tracking the user's activity as a side effect?

options.text: Explicit entry is a service to the user; side-effect tracking may serve conflicting interests
Explicit entry serves advertisers, while side-effect tracking serves only the user
Side-effect tracking is always harmless, because users benefit from the resulting features
Both are equally surveillance, since any stored data about a user amounts to tracking

questions.explanation: When a system stores only what users deliberately entered so it can process it as they wish, the user is the customer and the system performs a service. When activity is logged as a side effect of other actions, the service takes on interests of its own, which may conflict with the user's. Some tracking does benefit users (better search ranking, recommendations, A/B-tested interfaces), but depending on the business model, tracking often goes much further.

questions.question: When an online service is funded through advertising, what changes about the tracking of its users?

options.text: The advertisers become the customers, and users' interests come second
Advertising funding reduces the amount of tracking the service needs
Advertising funding limits tracking to what each ad strictly requires
Advertising funding makes the users into the service's real customers

questions.explanation: If advertising funds the service, the advertisers are the actual customers and users' interests take second place. Tracking becomes more detailed, analyses reach further, and data is retained for a long time to build detailed profiles for marketing. The user receives a free service and is coaxed into engaging as much as possible, while the tracking primarily serves advertisers, a relationship that can be described with the more sinister word 'surveillance'.

questions.question: Which thought experiment is suggested for exposing the true nature of large-scale data collection?

options.text: Replace the word 'data' with 'surveillance' in common industry phrases
Replace the word 'surveillance' with 'data' to make phrases sound neutral
Replace the word 'users' with 'customers' in common industry phrases
Replace the word 'tracking' with 'analytics' in common industry phrases

questions.explanation: Substituting 'surveillance' for 'data' turns 'data-driven organization', 'real-time data streams', 'data warehouse', and 'data scientists' into phrases that sound far less benign. The point is deliberately polemic: in making software 'eat the world', we have built the greatest mass surveillance infrastructure ever seen, with internet-connected microphones in smartphones, smart TVs, voice assistants, and even toys. The other substitutions keep or soften the neutral framing.

questions.question: How does today's corporate data collection compare with what repressive regimes have been able to achieve?

options.text: Repressive regimes could only dream of a microphone in every room and a tracker on everyone
It is far less extensive than the state surveillance of historical repressive regimes ever was
It is similar in reach, but the data is collected by governments rather than by corporations
It is less intrusive, because the collected data is used only for product recommendations

questions.explanation: Even the most repressive regimes could only dream of a microphone in every room and every person constantly carrying a location-tracking device, yet people adopt this voluntarily, even enthusiastically. The difference is that corporations rather than government agencies collect the data. People accept it because they feel they have nothing to hide or the purpose seems benign, but combined with predictive analytics that distinction becomes less clear.

questions.question: When does corporate surveillance start to appear less benign than merely better recommendations?

options.text: When it decides important outcomes, such as insurance coverage or employment
Only when it is carried out by government agencies rather than by companies
Never, since its purpose is only better recommendations and personalized marketing
Only when the collected data is sold on to third parties such as data brokers

questions.explanation: Car insurance premiums linked to in-car tracking devices and health coverage depending on wearing a fitness tracker show surveillance being used to decide important aspects of life. Data analysis can also reveal surprisingly intrusive things: a smartwatch's movement sensor can be used to infer what you type, including passwords, with fairly good accuracy, and analysis algorithms will only improve.

questions.question: A service argues that users consented to tracking by agreeing to its terms of service and privacy policy. What is wrong with this consent argument? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Users cannot consent meaningfully without understanding collection and use
One person's data can expose non-users who never consented
The service sets one-sided terms without genuine negotiation or reciprocity
Such consent is automatically invalid in every jurisdiction

questions.explanation: Users have little knowledge of what data they feed in or how it is retained and processed, and privacy policies obscure more than they illuminate, so consent is not meaningful. Data from one user often reveals things about other people who never agreed to any terms. And the relationship is one-way and asymmetric: there is no negotiation over how much data is provided and what is received in return, because the service sets the terms.

optionExplanations.a: Consent is not meaningful when people do not understand what is collected, inferred, retained, or shared. Clicking through an opaque policy is weak evidence of an informed choice.
optionExplanations.b: One user's contacts, photos, or genetic and social relationships can reveal facts about people who never joined the service. Their exposure cannot be justified by the first user's consent.
optionExplanations.c: A take-it-or-leave-it service contract offers little negotiation and the provider controls how terms evolve. This power imbalance makes the transaction unlike a genuinely reciprocal agreement.
optionExplanations.d: The critique is ethical and practical, not a claim that every consent mechanism is legally void everywhere. Jurisdictions and valid-consent requirements differ.

questions.question: For a user who objects to a service's tracking, why is 'just don't use it' not a genuinely free choice?

options.text: Opting out is costly when a service is essential for social participation
It is a free choice, since no online service is truly essential to anyone
Opting out is free for anyone who has read and understood the privacy policy
Opting out is impossible, because every service tracks non-users completely

questions.explanation: If a service is regarded by most people as essential for basic social participation (such as carrying a smartphone, socializing on Facebook, searching with Google), using it is de facto mandatory, and network effects add a social cost to declining. Opting out is realistic only for the privileged few with time and knowledge to understand the policy and who can afford to miss social or professional opportunities; for others, surveillance becomes inescapable.

questions.question: Some claim 'privacy is dead' because many people post personal details on social media. What is the correct response?

options.text: The claim is false: privacy means the freedom to choose what to reveal to whom
The claim is true: once people post personal details publicly, privacy has gone
The claim is false: privacy means keeping absolutely everything about oneself secret
The claim is beside the point: privacy is a property of data, not of people

questions.explanation: Having privacy does not mean keeping everything secret; it means having the freedom to choose which things to reveal to whom, what to make public, and what to keep secret. The right to privacy is a decision right that lets each person choose where to be on the spectrum between secrecy and transparency in each situation. Surveillance does not so much erode privacy as transfer that decision right from the individual to the data collector.

questions.question: Companies that collect surveillance data keep much of what they infer secret. Why?

options.text: Because revealing it would seem creepy and damage their business model
Because legal requirements forbid them from revealing any of it
Because the inferred data turns out to be commercially worthless
Because they delete each inference immediately after using it

questions.explanation: Revealing the outcome of surveillance would be perceived as creepy and would harm a business model that relies on knowing more about people than competitors do. Intimate information is revealed only indirectly, for example as tools for targeting ads to groups such as people with a particular illness. Even if users cannot be personally reidentified, they lose agency over disclosing such information: the company exercises the privacy right, aiming to maximize profit.

questions.question: Privacy settings let a user of an online service control which aspects of their data other users can see. What do they achieve, and what do they leave untouched?

options.text: They restrict what other users see, but not the service's own access and use
They restrict the service's own internal use, but not what other users can see
They restrict both other users' views and the service's own internal analysis
They restrict neither, and serve only as a notice to users about data handling

questions.explanation: Privacy settings are a starting point for handing some control back to users, but regardless of the setting the service itself has unfettered access to the data and may use it in any way permitted by its privacy policy. Even if it promises not to sell data to third parties, it usually grants itself unrestricted rights to process and analyze the data internally, often far beyond what users can see.

questions.question: When control over disclosure moves from an individual to a company collecting personal data, why is that transfer historically unprecedented?

options.text: Surveillance was expensive and manual, and trusted data use was governed by ethics and law
Surveillance is an entirely new phenomenon with no historical precedent of any kind
Trust relationships over sensitive personal information are an entirely new development
Data-protection law now forbids any transfer of control over personal data to companies

questions.explanation: Surveillance has always existed, but it was expensive and manual, not scalable and automated. Trust relationships also existed, such as between patient and doctor or defendant and attorney, but data use there was strictly governed by ethical, legal, and regulatory constraints. Internet services make it easy to amass huge amounts of sensitive information without meaningful consent and use it at massive scale, which makes this transfer of privacy rights historically unprecedented.

questions.question: Behavioural data is sometimes called 'data exhaust'. What does this term suggest, and what is a more accurate view?

options.text: That it is waste; yet if ads fund the service, it is the core asset
That it is waste, and rightly so, because behavioural data has no resale market
That it is the network traffic overhead created by tracking user activity
That it is the energy consumed by datacenters while storing user data

questions.explanation: 'Exhaust' implies a byproduct that would otherwise be thrown away, making analytics look like recycling. From an economic view it is the other way round: if targeted advertising pays for the service, behavioural data is its core asset and the application is merely a means of luring users into feeding in personal information. The existence of data brokers buying and reselling personal data, and startups valued by their 'eyeballs', support this view.

questions.question: Beyond the company that collected it, through which routes can personal data end up in other hands? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Governments obtaining it through secret deals, coercion, legal compulsion, or theft
Being sold as an asset when the collecting company goes bankrupt
Breaches by criminals or leaks by insiders, since data is hard to secure
Mandatory public release, which data-protection law requires after a fixed period

questions.explanation: Because personal data is valuable, many parties want it: governments may obtain it by secret deals, coercion, legal compulsion, or theft; it is sold as an asset if the company goes bankrupt; and it is hard to secure, so breaches happen disconcertingly often. Critics therefore call data a 'toxic asset' or 'hazardous material', and every collection decision must weigh benefits against the risk of the data falling into the wrong hands, including future management or regimes.

optionExplanations.a: Governments may compel disclosure lawfully, apply covert pressure, or simply steal data, so collected data becomes a target whose future political use the company cannot control.
optionExplanations.b: Personal data is among the assets sold when a company goes bankrupt, passing it to an organization users never chose and whose purposes may differ entirely.
optionExplanations.c: Data is difficult to secure against criminals, hostile intelligence services, and insiders, so breaches happen frequently; retaining sensitive data creates ongoing exposure.
optionExplanations.d: Data-protection law imposes purpose limitation and minimization, not compulsory publication of collected personal data; no such legal route exists. The real escape routes are government access, asset sales in bankruptcy, and breaches or leaks.

questions.question: Against what political horizon should decisions about collecting personal data be judged?

options.text: All possible future governments, not just today's political environment
Only the current legal and political environment in which the data is collected
Only the business requirements of the coming financial year
Only the stated retention period, regardless of which regimes may come later

questions.explanation: There is no guarantee that every future government will respect human rights and civil liberties, so 'it is poor civic hygiene to install technologies that could someday facilitate a police state'. Data collected now may persist and be compelled later. Knowledge is power, and scrutinizing others while avoiding scrutiny is an important form of power, which is why totalitarian governments want surveillance; technology companies also accumulate such power, much of it outside public oversight.

questions.question: Why is the Industrial Revolution used as a comparison for the information age's use of data?

options.text: Both brought major benefits alongside serious harms that took regulation to manage
Both were driven primarily by steam-powered machinery and heavy manufacturing
Both were purely beneficial, with no significant downsides for workers or society
Both were purely harmful, with no lasting economic benefits for anyone involved

questions.explanation: The Industrial Revolution brought sustained economic growth and better living standards, but also dreadful air and water pollution, harsh working conditions, and child labour. It took a long time to establish safeguards such as environmental regulation, workplace safety, and food inspections; they raised business costs but society benefited hugely. The information age similarly has major problems to confront, and the collection and use of data is one of them.

questions.question: Bruce Schneier compares data to something from an earlier industrial era. To what, and what follows for engineers?

options.text: To pollution: it festers like waste, and future generations will judge us
To capital: a pure asset with no downside, so engineers should collect all they can
To oil: a scarce extractable resource that engineers should refine
To electricity: a utility that should simply be metered and billed

questions.explanation: Schneier calls data the pollution problem of the information age, and protecting privacy the environmental challenge: almost all computers produce information that stays around, festering, and how we contain and dispose of it is central to the health of the information economy. Just as we now wonder how early industrialists ignored pollution, future generations will judge how we handled data collection and misuse. The implication for engineers is to treat collected data as a hazardous byproduct, minimizing and safeguarding it, rather than as a pure asset.

questions.question: The 1995 European Data Protection Directive places two requirements on personal data. Which?

options.text: Collected for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes; adequate, relevant, not excessive
Collected as broadly as possible; and retained indefinitely to allow later exploration
Collected only after paying the user for it; and deleted again within 24 hours
Collected only by public bodies; and never shared with or sold to any private company

questions.explanation: The 1995 Directive requires personal data to be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and not further processed incompatibly with them, and to be adequate, relevant, and not excessive for those purposes. These rules run directly counter to the Big Data philosophy of maximizing collection, combining datasets, and exploring for unforeseen insights, which is why the Directive's effectiveness in today's internet context is doubtful.

questions.question: Which changes are proposed for how the tech industry treats personal data?

options.text: Stop treating users as metrics, self-regulate, and educate users
Optimize engagement metrics harder, oppose regulation, and shorten policies
Wait for legislation, changing nothing voluntarily in the meantime
Collect more data but anonymize it, leaving policy to lawmakers

questions.explanation: The proposal is a culture shift: stop regarding users as metrics to be optimized and remember they are humans who deserve respect, dignity, and agency; self-regulate data collection and processing to establish and maintain users' trust; and educate end users about how their data is used rather than keeping them in the dark. Regulation can help, but culture and attitude changes are necessary too.

questions.question: Individuals' right to control their own data is likened to the natural environment of a national park. Which claim does that analogy make?

options.text: Without explicit protection, privacy will be destroyed in a tragedy of the commons
Each individual alone can fully protect their own privacy, like a private garden
Ubiquitous surveillance is inevitable, so people must simply adapt to it
Privacy protects itself, because users abandon invasive services

questions.explanation: Like a national park, individual control over data will be destroyed unless it is explicitly protected and cared for; the result would be a tragedy of the commons in which everyone is worse off. Ubiquitous surveillance is not inevitable and can still be stopped. Starting points include not retaining data forever but purging it once no longer needed, and enforcing access control through cryptographic protocols rather than merely by policy.

questions.question: Which statements about legislation and self-regulation of personal data are reasonable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The 1995 EU Data Protection Directive's effectiveness in today's internet context is doubtful
Industry should self-regulate its data practices even as updated regulations are developed
Overregulation could block beneficial uses, such as medical data analysis
Ubiquitous surveillance is inevitable, so regulation is pointless

questions.explanation: The Directive's purpose-limitation rules conflict with Big Data's exploratory philosophy, so its effectiveness is doubtful, and updated regulations are being developed. Companies oppose regulation as a burden, which is partly justified: analysis of medical data might prevent deaths through better diagnostics, and overregulation could prevent such breakthroughs, so risks and opportunities must be balanced. The industry should also self-regulate to maintain trust. Surveillance is not inevitable; it can still be stopped.

optionExplanations.a: Purpose limitation and data minimization run directly counter to collecting broadly and exploring for unforeseen insights, so it is doubtful the 1995 Directive works well for today's internet.
optionExplanations.b: Law lags technology and cannot specify every responsible design choice, so organizations should limit their own collection and processing to maintain users' trust while regulation evolves.
optionExplanations.c: Medical data carries clear privacy risks but also the potential to find better diagnostics and treatments, so regulation that is too strict could prevent real benefits; the two must be balanced.
optionExplanations.d: Ubiquitous surveillance is a result of design and policy choices, not a technical inevitability, so it can still be stopped and regulation is not pointless.

questions.question: You are about to add indefinite behavioral event tracking to a consumer app. On data-ethics grounds, what should change? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Retention: purge data as soon as it is no longer needed
Purpose: collect only for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes
Transparency: educate users about how their data is used
Scale: collect as much as possible now, since storage is cheap

questions.explanation: Indefinite behavioural tracking maximizes the harm data can do: the longer data is kept and the vaguer its purpose, the greater the risk of breaches, misuse, and reuse by future owners or governments. Data-ethics practice therefore asks for purpose limitation (collect only for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes), short retention (purge data once it is no longer needed), and transparency (educate users about how their data is used), ideally with access enforced by cryptographic mechanisms rather than policy alone. Cheap storage lowers the monetary cost of collection, not its privacy or security risk, so it is not a justification for collecting everything.

optionExplanations.a: Data should not be retained forever but purged once it is no longer needed; indefinitely kept behavioural history increases breach and misuse risk without a concrete present benefit.
optionExplanations.b: Purpose limitation lets users and reviewers judge whether collection is justified and prevents later incompatible reuse; an unspecified possible future use is not a legitimate purpose.
optionExplanations.c: Users have little knowledge of what is collected, and privacy policies obscure more than they illuminate, so plain explanations are needed for any consent to be meaningful.
optionExplanations.d: Cheap storage lowers monetary cost but not privacy, security, discrimination, or political risk; collecting everything turns hypothetical future value into certain present exposure.

questions.question: Access control over personal data can rest on policy or on mechanism. Which is preferable, and how is it enforced?

options.text: Mechanism: enforce access through cryptographic protocols, not policy alone
Policy: a clearly written, published privacy policy is the strongest control
Obscurity: keep the schema undocumented so outsiders cannot write queries
Neither: access control conflicts with immutability and has to be dropped

questions.explanation: A privacy policy is only a promise that the organization can break, change, or fail to enforce. Enforcing access control through cryptographic protocols, so that data can be read only by parties holding the right keys, makes the restriction a property of the system rather than of goodwill. This is proposed alongside purging data once it is no longer needed; deletion conflicts with immutable logs, but that issue can be solved. Obscurity is not access control.

questions.question: When dataflows are expressed as transformations from one dataset to another, how can you change a processing step (such as an index's structure) or recover from a bug?

options.text: Rerun the new or fixed code over the whole input to rederive the output
Only append new processing steps, since existing outputs can never be changed
Restore the derived dataset from a backup taken before the change
Hand-edit the existing derived output in place to match the new logic

questions.explanation: Because each derived dataset is produced by deterministic transformation code from retained input, changing a step (for example the structure of an index or cache) just means running the new code over the whole input dataset to rederive the output. Likewise, if something goes wrong, you fix the code and reprocess the data to recover. Backups or manual patches would preserve or compound the bug rather than recompute a correct result.

questions.question: In dataflow systems, how can strong integrity guarantees be achieved scalably without distributed transactions?

options.text: End-to-end operation IDs for idempotence, plus asynchronous constraint checking
Distributed transactions across all systems, which alone can provide integrity
Synchronized clocks that order every write, so conflicting writes can be discarded
Making every client wait synchronously for every constraint check before writing

questions.explanation: End-to-end operation identifiers make operations idempotent, so retries and replays cannot apply an effect twice, and constraints are checked asynchronously. Clients can either wait until the check has passed or go ahead without waiting and risk having to apologize for a violation. This is much more scalable and robust than distributed transactions, fits how many business processes work, and avoids most (not all) coordination, while audits verify integrity and detect corruption. Synchronized clocks cannot reliably order writes, and making every client wait for every check reintroduces the coordination the design avoids.

questions.question: Which harms can follow from the collection and use of data about people? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Decisions that seriously affect people's lives and are hard to appeal
Discrimination and exploitation of people
Normalized surveillance and exposure of intimate information
Higher infrastructure costs and slower software

questions.explanation: Data can be used to do good, but it can also do significant harm: justifying decisions that seriously affect people's lives and are difficult to appeal, leading to discrimination and exploitation, normalizing surveillance, and exposing intimate information. Data breaches and unintended consequences of well-intentioned uses add to the risk. Engineers carry a responsibility to work toward a world that treats people with humanity and respect.

optionExplanations.a: Opaque automated decisions can deny credit, employment, insurance, or services while leaving the affected person unable to understand or challenge the reason.
optionExplanations.b: Models trained on biased history can reproduce or amplify unequal treatment, and data about people's circumstances can be used to exploit vulnerable groups. Scale magnifies these harms.
optionExplanations.c: Routine tracking makes surveillance socially normal, while detailed datasets expose relationships, health, beliefs, and behaviour. The injury extends beyond technical confidentiality.
optionExplanations.d: Infrastructure cost and performance matter operationally, but they are not harms done to the people the data describes, which is what the ethical concern is about. A cheap, fast system can still be deeply harmful.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the proposed approach to building future data systems?

options.text: Derive views asynchronously from systems of record, keep integrity end to end, and audit
Use one distributed database with serializable transactions for every piece of data
Abandon derived data in favour of synchronous updates to every system at write time
Optimize for performance first, ahead of correctness and the ethics of data use

questions.explanation: Designate systems of record and derive indexes, views, and models from them through asynchronous, loosely coupled transformations, so faults stay local and reprocessing enables evolution. Maintain integrity with end-to-end operation IDs and asynchronous constraint checks instead of distributed transactions, and audit to detect corruption. Throughout, consider the effects on people: data systems should treat people with humanity and respect.
